subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
In my remarks yesterday when
discussing the principle of this bill I tried to show the trend in the dried fish industry in particular and its effect on my constituency.
I referred to reasons for the decline in the industry in years gone by, and stated 'hat
Salt Fish Board

the effectiveness of competition from the salt cod industry of foreign countries was the major factor in the decline in our market. This was brought about in two ways: first, by subsidies and assistance given by foreign governments to the industry generally, and, second, by government regulation to improve quality and marketability. These factors have been particularly effective since 1920.
The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud), in introducing the bill, referred to the trend since the days of the war or the year I have just mentioned. It was at that time that the vicious circle in which we now find ourselves started, and we are still confined within its bounds. During the period of the war, owing to disturbances in Europe interfering both with the fishing grounds and European fishing operations, there was in Canada a favourable reaction upon our fishing industry. There was increased demand and prices went up. After the war, however, European fish-producing countries reorganized their industry, and since that time they seem constantly to have gained ground to our disadvantage.
The government of Norway voted 83,000,000 as bounties for the three year period beginning in 1920. The sum of $600,000 was spent in securing the Havana market alone. We saw the fish of Norway quoted at extremely low prices in competition with us in markets where we thought we were firmly entrenched. Iceland made serious inroads in the markets of Spain and Italy particularly, offering more or less high grade salt fish at very low prices. Foreign countries not only helped by 'bonuses and Dounties; they also made regulations for inspection, and brought about much improvement in fish curing.
Norway, besides the help I have indicated, continued for a number of years to help by way of regulation and inspection, and was paying a bonus of at least $1 a quintal. France was paying $2 per quintal, and Denmark $1. It is understood that Norway paid $1,000,000 during 1937 in subsidizing this export, and $1,750,000 in 1938.
In 1921, when this trend started, a Canadian trade commissioner predicted that the markets which had been monopolized by Canada for the five preceding years would soon be lost if steps were not taken to help us to compete with foreign countries. Unfortunately that was true, and it was what brought about the conditions which now prevail. In some markets the process of our elimination came about in a secondary way: European producing countries shoved Newfoundland out, and, in turn, Newfoundland came in and interfered with our markets, so that by each of these circumstances we were being caught in the vicious circle which I have described,
rMr Pottier.]
I should like to refer hon. members to one interesting report given annually by Hawes & Company, an English concern of worldwide experience in the industry. They show what has happened as a result of these assistances and subsidies given by foreign countries. For convenience I compare the years 1919 and 1927. Norway, for example, in 1919 produced in fresh cod alone 359 million pounds; by 1927 their production had increased to 808 million pounds. The production of the Faroe islands, which in 1919 amounted to 99 million pounds, increased by 1927 to 103 million pounds. Iceland produced 168 million pounds in 1919 and 362 million pounds in 1927. Germany's production of 28 million pounds in 1919 had risen by 1927 to 110 million pounds. In France the increase was from 73 million pounds to 124 million pounds over the same period; in England the increase was from 173 million pounds to 328 million pounds. And this trend has continued. I give the figures for those two years because, so to speak, they split the period half way, indicating what the trend has been and how it has continued. In the same period our production dropped from 260 million pounds to 197 million pounds, and by 1932 had dropped further to 142 million pounds. So that where the other countries gained, we lost. This condition is a result of intensive assistance by way of bounties, subsidies and market regulations put into effect by countries.
Unfortunately in the salt fish industry there are no new markets. There are certain people throughout the world who eat salt fish, and there is no change in the consuming market in that respect. The only fluctuations in the salt fish trade are brought about by changes in the purchasing power of the people who are accustomed to eat and apparently need salt fish particularly in the warmer countries. Taking the world as a whole, there are no new countries to which we can look for markets in the immediate future, no other consuming classes who are likely to start eating salt fish. The only way we can hope to increase the income to our fishermen from this industry is to find our way back into the markets which we formerly had and which we lost through assistance given by foreign governments to their industry and to our disadvantage. We must take some steps to try to get back what we have lost, or even to hold what we have at the present time. This bill which is now before the house is designed for that purpose. I think it will be as effective as anything the government could bring in to assist this industry.
I did not mention that this bill covers all salt fish, including boneless herring, mack-

Salt Fish Board
erel, pollock and hake. These are not small items. For instance, in boneless cod the value was $175,000; pickled codfish, about $300,000; pickled and salted herring, $400,000; mackerel, $400,000; pollock and hake, about $40,000. All these will be affected by this bill, in addition to the dried codfish to which I have been referring up to the present. I have not mentioned these other types of fish that will be affected by this measure because I believe the dried codfish industry has been a backlog, so to speak, of the fishing industry in the maritime provinces. With the trend going down, as I indicated, we suffered severely; and we must try to reverse that trend, which will be to the benefit of the people generally.
It seems to me there are limits to the benefits that can be derived' by fishermen generally from the fresh fish trade, and in our lobster industry difficulties are constantly arising. Under present conditions in the fresh fish trade you must have two things; the fisherman must be comparatively near the fishing grounds, particularly the shore fisherman, and he must live in a district reasonably near his market. Fresh fish must be transported quickly; otherwise it will spoil on its way to the market. In the salt fish trade, however, the situation is entirely different. The fisherman brings his fish ashore and salts them, and then he can keep them indefinitely, for a week, a month, or longer. That enables the fisherman in the outlying districts to cany on where it would be impossible for him to do so if he were engaged in the fresh fish trade.
I should have stated that Newfoundland found itself in exactly the same position at a somewhat earlier period. Away back in 1936 they established a fisheries board which at present is practically a marketing board. It assists the fishermen financially, more or less controls exports and tries in every way to improve the marketing of the product. I think, therefore, the time has definitely come when we must take some such action as is proposed in this measure. There are two sets of individuals who will be affected by this legislation, the shore fishermen and the schooner fishermen. I hope this bill will benefit both classes, and that the shore fishermen particularly will be encouraged to carry on. The man in the outlying district who is too far from the market to engage in the fresh fish trade can and will produce salt fish if he can sell it at prices that will bring him a reasonable return.
I realize that there may be difficulties in the selection of a board. This is not a pleasant thing for me to mention, but I think it my duty to give my views on the subject. I do not desire to embarrass the government, but I must urge upon the minister that no person should be appointed to the board who is directly or indirectly interested in the export of fish. It can easily be seen how difficult and impossible it would be for an exporter of salt fish to sit on a board that is passing out government money to assist in the export of that fish. I do not care how fair a man might try to be; human nature has too many frailties to be put to a test of that kind. I want to see on the board men who are particularly sympathetic to the fishermen. The quality of human understanding possessed by the members of the board, together with their executive ability, will largely determine the success of the measure now under consideration. I hope the price to the fisherman will be increased to a point where it will be sufficient to enable him to carry on, and I trust the board will have that in mind in mapping out a definite policy.
We have in this measure a definite plan. How many years have we heard people say, "Oh. something has to be done about the fishing industry." But inevitably when you ask what should be done the answer was "I don't know." In 1935 the then leader of the government said at Bridgewater: "I confess I do not know what is the remedy." From across the floor of the house we have heard, "Something has to be done," but never have we had a definite plan suggested. In this measure we have a definite indication of what the government proposes to do. As I have said previously, the time has come when the fishing industry must be looked at specifically with a view to making definite decisions in regard to it. The step now being taken is definite and specific and looks towards the development of our fisheries. I believe we have become seized with the extent and possibilities of our fisheries resources and that we are now showing an intention of dealing with them in the same manner as we deal with the other primary products of this country. I realize, as I think every reasonable Canadian must realize, that there are limits beyond which we cannot go. The government must not be wasteful, and new fields must be broken cautiously. I intend to stress before my constituents the benefits derived under this bill, to argue that it is fair and reasonable and that they should take advantage of it. I see it as a new experience, holding forth great hope and containing great possibilities. I am convinced that the fishermen generally will see the merits of the legislation and will do their share to bring about greater production and increased prosperity.
I want to express to the government, and particularly to the minister, the appreciation of my constituents in respect of this legislation. I think the minister has d"T,e more-and I
Salt Fish Board

say this advisedly because I believe it should be brought to the fore-than any other minister of fisheries we have ever had. He has wrestled with the situation and has striven to bring about a definite policy of economic planning; by which I mean that this is the first legislation brought before the House of Commons in the interests of fishermen that has involved any element of economic planning. The minister has made of the Department of Fisheries a real department. I beg hon. members to approve the bill as an evidence to our fishermen that their difficulties are being considered, and that we are working with frankness and harmony of purpose in extending to them a helping hand.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a bill entitled "An act to provide for the constitution of a salt fish board," and it has for its primary purpose the improvement of conditions among and the bringing of greater returns to the primary producers. There are other provisions, but, as I see it, the heart of the bill is in paragraph (b) of section 5, which says:
5. The board shall . . .
(b) devise and recommend to the minister a plan, or plans, which may be adopted for the orderly marketing of fish, salt or to be salted, with a view to improving conditions and bringing greater returns to the primary produce and the exporter.
I believe the word "produce" is incorrect; it should have an "r" added, making the word "producer."
The bill contains also power to investigate and report. In addition there is the item of $800,000 in the supplementary estimates to provide for assisting the salt fish branch of the fishing industry. I believe that this item in the estimates, and the appointment of the salt fish board are two vital factors which will tend to improve conditions in the industry.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), for whom I have the highest regard, and on whose opinions I place great value, has criticized the appointment of a board. He has said that it simply looks like the appointment of another board and further expenditure by the country which could not be justified. I have heard expressions of opinion from people in Nova Scotia and elsewhere to the effect that with its own staff the Department of Fisheries could carry out the work for which the board would be appointed. I should like to point out, however, that for a long time we have had ministers of fisheries at the head of the Department of Fisheries, and yet successive governments have failed to deal effectively with the matter. Moreover, at its last session the legislature of Nova
*Mr. Pottier.]
Scotia passed a resolution asking for the appointment of a resident deputy minister of fisheries in Nova Scotia, indicating that in that province there is a feeling that local knowledge should be brought to bear on fisheries matters, and that there should be more attention paid to the fisheries in that part of the country.
I am informed that there is a provincial fish board in British Columbia, and I have no doubt that that board, appointed by the British Columbia legislature, would cooperate with the dominion government as it sees fit in the interests of British Columbia fisheries.
There is this to be said about a board: It seems to be part of the necessary equipment of a democracy. It is always well in bringing forward something new for the benefit of an industry to call in technical experts who are interested in the industry. While at the present time in Canada the appointment of boards is criticized, I would point out that we are not overloaded with them in the maritime provinces. The appointment of a board would be an added advantage to the maritimes in presenting their claims to the government and in persistently and intelligently pressing those claims, as is done in western Canada.
I do not think the members of the board should be highly paid. I believe there are men in Nova Scotia who, for the sake of seiving the public and the industry, would readily serve on a board of this kind. These are men who have been successful in the industry, who would not depend for their daily bread wholly upon any fee they might receive for their services, and who do not demand a high standard of living. I do not think we need any $5,000 a year man, or anything of the kind, on the board. Such service should be considered an honour, and I am confident that the men chosen would gladly cooperate with the department and the government in the interest of the fisheries of the province.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier) has suggested that no one either directly or indirectly connected with the export of fish should be on the board. Well, as I read the bill, if we eliminate those who are interested in or who have been connected with the export and production of fish we should have no one left but members of the learned professions, without practical experience. So far as possible I believe we should confine the appointments to men in the fishing industry.

speechtext:
Both the fishermen and the exporters are financially interested in the fishing industry. In the county I represent we believe that there should be real cooperation between capital and labour, and that it should not be a class movement. Every person connected with the fishing industry has a financial interest in it. I contend that in order to have the benefit of expert knowledge and the best advice available, we must get it from people who know the business. In choosing the board the minister should maintain a proper balance between primary producers and exporters, and should select men who will work together and produce the best results for the fishing industry of the Atlantic coast.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni mentioned the Halifax award, which by legislation now provides the bounty paid to the fishermen. In his customary persistent and eloquent fashion he put forward an argument in the interests of the British Columbia fishermen. I shall not discuss that angle of the question at the present time, because it is not at issue. I would refer the hon. member, however, to the Maclean report, which goes so far as to say that there is no question as to the intent, and that the law should be amended to make it clear that the application of the bounty should be exclusively to fishermen on the Atlantic coast. The salmon fishing industry constitutes the major portion of fishing on the Pacific coast, and the regulations particularly show that salmon fishermen are not included among those who should receive the benefits on the Atlantic coast.

speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member that the act should be amended so that the meaning would be clear.
This bill is of great importance to my constituency. In 1937 there were 203,000 quintals of dried salt fish produced in Nova Scotia. Of that amount 104,150 quintals were produced in Lunenburg, where I live. For over fifty years Lunenburg has been the commercial centre of the deep sea salt fish industry of Canada. The achievements in that regard have contributed to making this county one of the most stable in the country, and this has had its effect on provincial and national
life.	.
The bill provides that assistance may be given not to exceed twenty-five per cent of the value
of the fish at the point and time of export shall be provided from the item in the supplementary estimates. This morning I received a telegram from my riding stating that the price is likely to be $4.50 for large fish, $2.50 for haddock and $2 for hake. This is the price paid to the primary producer, and when consideration is given to the expenses that must be incurred before the fish is ready for export, it is easy to see that twenty-five per cent will amount to well over $1 per quintal. For the last three years the government of Nova Scotia has paid a bounty on fish. For two years it was SI, and then it was reduced to 75 cents, 50 cents going to the fisherman and 25 cents to the vessel owner. This year it is expected the federal government will provide stimulation for the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast.
In 1937 the production of salted fish in Lunenburg was increased by about twenty-five per cent, partly due to the bounty which was paid. Without that bounty the fishermen could not have operated at a profit. This cost the provincial government perhaps $80,000, but it brought into this country over $300,000 of new wealth. When you can create over $300,000 of new wealth with an expenditure of $80,000, it is not only good for the fishermen, it is good for the country. We have a tariff structure to assist and stimulate our manufacturing industry. We must consider that the primary producer is the customer who buys the articles manufactured in this country. Unless the primary producer has money he cannot buy. I think it can well be seen how this stimulation of a primary industry is justified. The manufacturing sections of this country are the sections that have prospered. There is a greater per capita wealth in those districts, and the people have more purchasing power. They have greater earning power than the people engaged in our primary industry on the coast. I am sure if we follow the example of what has been done for the manufacturing industry, we shall bring about greater prosperity in this primary industry and we shall have what might be called a balanced.economy.
Reference has been made to the fresh fish industry being included in this bill. This is a matter that will probably be considered in committee. It is something about which even our fishermen are not quite sure, and I do not think we can be dogmatic in deciding a question of this kind. This bill is the first step forward, and I think we should go carefully. I am supporting the principle of the bill because its intention is to raise the standard of living of our primary producers in the province of Nova Scotia. I consider

Salt Fish Board

section 5, paragraph (b) to be the heart of the bill. This board to be created will no doubt have to fix the price of the product. I might say that the price of salted fish is usually arrived at definitely in the province of Nova Scotia three times a year. The first occasion is the frozen bait trip. This price has already been paid and everybody knows what it is. Then there is the spring trip, the prices for which have not yet been arrived at because these fish are not landed or ready for market. Then there will be the summer trip. When prices are agreed upon, everyone knows what they are. I believe the intention of this bill is to set prices for each of these seasonal productions. In that way the primary producer, the fisherman, will be guaranteed an amount from the money voted by this parliament.
The bill has been framed so that the primary producer will get his share of the money used to stimulate this industry. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni expressed the thought that perhaps it would all go to the exporter, but let me say to him that so far as I am concerned, representing as I do the banner fishing constituency of the Dominion of Canada-[DOT]

Mr. Speaker, there are two criticisms I have to make of this bill. It is not my intention to deal with them at any great length, but let me say that it is not to be wondered at if we from British Columbia should offer a protest, mild though it be, to the putting into effect of a bill designed to help the fishermen of the maritimes alone. I say this because British Columbia produces at least fifty per cent of the total catch of all fish in Canada.
It produces more by nearly $3,000,000 than the
[Mr. KioW.J
two provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick combined, the figures for 1937-38 being: British Columbia, $16,150,439; New Brunswick, $4,449,688, and Nova Scotia, $9,229,834.
My own view, Mr. Speaker, is that this bill makes a new departure in singling out the maritime provinces for special treatment. The bill is designed especially for the two maritime provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. We realize that the fishermen on that coast do require help; but so also do the fishermen of British Columbia. While every effort will be made as a result of this bill to increase the export of dried salt fish, I think a greater effort should be made to increase the consumption of fresh fish in Canada. I think that should come first. True, the department is spending something like $200,000 a year in advertising fish, but will the mere advertising of fish in magazines and newspapers result in a greater consumption of fish in the eastern central, and prairie provinces if the fish, when they reach the consumer, are not in first class condition. I hear many complaints around Ottawa, even from members of parliament, about the quality of the fish they purchase in this city. They like fish, but they are off fish after eating it in Ottawa and in many eastern cities. Fish has to be very fresh, and with the new methods of freezing and rapid transportation there is no reason why there should not be an increased consumption of fresh fish in Canada. I believe greater efforts should be made along that line. It might interest members to know that Canada consumes per head only from 20 to 22 pounds of fish, as compared with 40 pounds in Great Britain, 70 pounds in Norway, 92 pounds in Japan, and 25 pounds in Germany. We have in the maritime provinces and in British Columbia great fisheries. Yet all governmental efforts are concentrated on inducing people abroad to eat our fish, quite overlooking the great market we have at home. As I say, I believe a further effort should be made to increase the consumption of fish in Canada.
This bill does not affect and will not help the fishermen of British Columbia, although we have an export trade in salted fish to the old country and to other countries as well. True, we had a fish board in British Columbia, but it was controlled mostly by Japanese interests, because most of the salted fish exported from British Columbia and controlled by that board went to the orient, either to Japan or to China. But there is a considerable market in Great Britain for our finer varieties of salmon caught by trailers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fishing industry in Canada must be in a bad way, judging from the addresses which have been made in the house during the present session. I am glad that the people in the maritimes are veering around to the policy and principles of protection, the old national policy, for the protection of this basic industry w'hich has suffered so much, and that at last a form of needed bonuses, subventions and subsidies is to be set up.
I am sorry to see that the bill proposes to create another board to assist in the preparation and marketing of fish. It was contended, when the old Department of Marine and Fisheries, which had existed since 1867, was divided and a separate minister appointed in charge of fisheries, that the change would put the fishing industry, which had been suffering for years, on a sound basis. This will be the second board appointed by the federal government to deal with fish. The late government appointed a board under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act to assist, those engaged in the fishing industry. Now we are to have another board, a board with power to appoint advisory committees of all kinds, to make rules and regulations, and to have a duplicate staff, which will no doubt be independent of the department. Then you will have two rival bodies having authority to deal with fisheries, the minister and his 71482-2SS1
staff, and the two boards and their staffs, with all the consequent useless duplication.
I am glad to see maritime members supporting at last the principle of bonuses, subventions and subsidies for this industry, which I have advocated since 1922, just as they did, after a long fight, for coal, steel and iron. The principle is also applied to grain. I believe that the proper solution for our problems in the basic industries in all the provinces is to be found in the application of the principles of the old national policy, of which the party on this side of the house and its predecessors were' the founders and authors and pioneers.
I fail to see, Mr. Speaker, how another agency, the board to be set up under this bill, will help to solve the problem. We have the national railways, and we have boats under the marine department, and there is no reason why a long range plan could not be worked out so that our transportation facilities would be utilized far more than they have been for the quick transportation of fish, inland and for export. We have an exhibition of fish at the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto, but the market for dried, salted and pickled fish has never been what it should have been, or what it was hoped it would be.
The bill overlooks one of the main reasons for the depression in this industry, and that is the inroads that machinery has made in this industry in the past ten or fifteen years. No board can change that condition; it is here to stay, and some of the evils which flow from the elimination of man power in this industry could be taken care of without a board at all. I fail to see why the country should be loaded with another board which will be a further burden on the taxpayer, adding to our over-government and overtaxation. This industry has not benefited very much from the boards which have already been set up, except that of the last government. In my opinion it is 'better for the minister of the crown to take responsibility for the proper preparation of the fish for market and for finding markets for it and giving aid to those in distress. There is also the Department of Trade and Commerce, which could help coordinate in marketing and preparation. Why all this duplication and overgovernment in this industry? Every good citizen in Canada wants to see proper support given to the fishing industry. I know that the people in the maritimes are suffering from conditions in the fishing industry, and there is a very warm feeling in Ontario for them. I have seen the conditions myself. But a board is not the cure for the disease. A minister of the crown has been specially appointed to
Salt Fish Board

look after the fisheries of this country, the responsibility should be left to him, and he should have a free hand to act and get results.
The people of the maritimes have been to blame, in part; for they have consistently supported free trade. Many of the big industries of the maritimes, coal, fish, steel and iron, have moved their head offices to Montreal and until recently the banks as well; and the industries have suffered in consequence.
It is a retrograde step for parliament to be appointing all these outside boards with power to make rules and regulations which are given the force of a statute, and boards with power to appoint additional advisory committees of all kinds. An advisory committee may be appointed in every riding to prepare the fish and help in finding a market for it. This bill overlooks something no board or anyone else in Canada can do, and is one of the real reasons for the condition of this industry, namely the fact that in Canada the fisheries are a declining factor consequent upon the fact that a maximum of mechanical development and a minimum of human power are responsible for the present depression in the industry.

When my hon. friend makes a statement of that sort in this house, following the rules of evidence, observed in any court he must have personal knowledge. If he is a fisherman within the meaning of this bill, and he received a cheque, then the statement is in order and can be accepted. But if he is speaking of what someone told him, it is not evidence, and as far as I am concerned, while I do not doubt his veracity for one single moment, I think there is a mistake somewhere. The mistake is not in my statement, because the fact remains that the money was claimed by the owners of the vessels, and the men who were fishing on those vessels said they were not entitled to receive it because they were receiving agreed rates; their board was being paid and in some cases some of them had a share in the vessel. The thing I am particularly interested in is in no wise of a selfish character, and I do not think it is so in the case of any hon. gentleman who has spoken or will speak in this house in regard to this matter. But when it comes to paying out of the treasury of Canada through the finance minister, governed by the supplementary estimates, a sum estimated at $800,000 this year, there should be a hard and fast, not a loose, wide open clause, through which you can drive a coach and four before you even begin to get an interpretation as to what it means. Take the constituency represented by myself and my colleague the hon. junior member for Halifax, who is here, who takes an interest in these matters; in the county of Halifax we have practically no fishermen except inshore fishermen unless they go down to Lunenburg and join some vessel.
It has been suggested that under this bill the pathway of the fishermen will be made 
rosy. Perhaps in order to get a full understanding of what may happen we should bear in mind what took place last winter, when the lobster fishermen were in such dire straits that they hardly knew where their next meal was coming from or how to keep themselves warm. What happened? This concerns persons both within and without this house, so that in what I have to say I am not casting any personal aspersions. After all, however, a department and a minister can be judged only according to the record, and we find that the assistance offered these people in their awful plight was this: they were offered snow shovels, picks and axes to go out and dig side drains and shovel snow in the middle of winter, so that they might get their lobster traps in order to carry on what is a fairly lucrative business with the United States and upper Canadian markets open to the lobster fishermen of our province. I say that could not have happened if proper legislation had been upon the statute book. We also find that in order to help the fishermen the provincial government desired to spend something like $177,000 on preliminary work on highways, and that in the middle of winter. Quite properly this government and the Minister of Fisheries took the position that this money could not be used for that purpose, and that unless the provincial government could devise some other method by means of which these men could earn what was required, the money would not be available. I understand, however, that a large portion of that money has been handed over to the province, which did not put up a dollar, and that S75 or $100 has been loaned to individual fishermen. Up to the present, however, I do not believe any hon. member of this house knows who spent that money, how it was spent, and who received it.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that when public moneys of Canada are voted by this house in order to help those engaged in a particular industry in time of distress and need, at least hon. members who have the responsibility of voting the money on the recommendation of the government and the responsible minister should have some information as to what has become of the money, who got it, how much has been spent and how much was put up by the provincial government. Up to the present that information has not been made available, and I do not believe it will be.
There is another condition which I. say should not be permitted to continue. To-day we have a department of fisheries without a deputy minister, without the king-pin of the

Salt Fish Board
department in his place in the Hunter building, guiding the destinies of the fishermen of Nova Scotia to the extent that the government can help them through money voted by this house as bonuses, cash grants or whatever they may be called. We have in the department a very capable gentleman, Mr. Cowie, whom I have known for years, but who is to retire very shortly. Since Mr. Found retired on reaching the age limit nothing has been done in the way of a new appointment, and I should like to know from the minister who is responsible for this legislation. As the minister in charge of the department of course'he is ultimately responsible, but I mean who in the department is responsible for the drafting of the legislation, and who asked for it? Yesterday the minister spoke of receiving letters from some person up along the baie de Chaleur who could not get rid of his fresh fish and did not know what to do, and from some other company. But there was nothing of finality, nothing in sequence produced by the minister yesterday to assist hon. members to come to any sound conclusion as to whether we were doing the right thing in the right way at this time.
Yesterday I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), who has devoted many years to the best interests of the people of his province and his constituency, whose heart to them is dearer than Pluto's mine, richer than gold. He placed before us certain claims and made certain suggestions, and he was speaking as an individual not directly interested in this industry. That is a very different thing from hearing from gentlemen whose first principle is to get all they can and give very little in return; who find out in the probate office how much their friend who died was worth and then try to make a little more money so that when their time is up they may beat him out in the matter of worldly wealth.
I am afraid my remarks have been somewhat rambling, but they could not be otherwise. I must confess, and I do so openly, that we have not had sufficient time to ascertain the intention, whether expressed or implied, of those who will have the task of putting this legislation into effect if it becomes law. I do not believe my colleague from Halifax desires, nor do I, to take a narrow view of this matter, or to view it purely from the standpoint of our constituency. But by a circuitous route and by inference we are told, "Oh, the primary producer will be all right, because he will have to sell to the exporter who will get the market." If one looks at the interpretation clause in the bill
he will find that the fisherman is the exporter. Then when we come to the section which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni said yesterday he would move to strike out, when in committee, we find that it is the exporter and not the fisherman who gets the twenty-five per cent. I say the exporter is not the fisherman, and I do not believe there is an hon. member in the house who will say for one moment that under the terms of the bill, or under the widest possible interpretation of its provisions an exporter is a fisherman in any sense of the word, although in the spring of the year he may go fishing for a little relaxation. He may bring home a few trout or a salmon to his wife and family. If he does not have good luck and happens to have a few dollars in his pocket, he will buy a couple of fish so that he will not have to come home and say, "Well, I had bad luck."
The situation to-day is serious. It is as serious for the fisherman in Nova Scotia as for the farmer in the Canadian west. Every hon. member in the house sympathizes with them. Not long ago I was told about conditions in Saskatchewan, and a vivid description was given to me of the dust bowl and of conditions which existed after storms had blown themselves out. I was told about the dire distress and need of people who had taken land in order that they might make a living and have happy homes. My heart goes out to them, as it does to the fishermen in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and the other provinces interested in fishing. I think every bona fide fisherman, who can be described as such within the finest meaning of the term, should have the same treatment as the fishermen in Nova Scotia and in my own constituency of Halifax.
It is my judgment that when this bill is read clause by clause and discussed in committee hon. members will realize how empty it is, with the exception of the fact that $800,000 is available for a purpose which should be specified, but which is not at all specific, either in the interpretation clause or under the other sections of the bill.
I dislike dealing with a matter which verges on personalities, but I should like to point out that when last winter public opinion was running so high, when petitions bearing 1,400 names came from Nova Scotia asking for assistance for fishermen who, through an act of God, were in a dire plight, they asked for bread and we gave them a stone. I do not know who has asked for this legislation. I heard the minister say yesterday that he had had representations in reference to beam trawlers. Last year I attended a meeting of
Salt Fish Board

the maritime union of fishermen, representative of fishermen from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick-Prince Edward Island had a separate meeting-and at that meeting, within my hearing, and within the hearing of the minister and Mr. Found, who were sitting there, I listened to a resolution asking that licences for beam trawlers be abolished forthwith or within a reasonable time. No explanation was given at that time by the minister, nor was any statement made as to future policies. That resolution, bearing the written word of the fishermen of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, was passed unanimously; and yet no more attention was paid to it than might be paid to a whiff of wind which might blow past the parliament buildings on a cold night. One can come in out of the cold to a place where it is warm. But when a few letters came to the minister from some private interests stating that they want a bonus of twenty-five per cent to find markets to which to ship the fish they buy from the fishermen, some attention is given to it. If twenty-five per cent is to be paid to the exporter, then I say there should be a parallel clause stating what the fisherman is to get who goes to sea and risks his life catching fish. It was astounding to find last winter that a member of the economic council of Nova Scotia, an adviser of the government in matters connected with fishing, was in favour of the trawlers, and was doing his best to keep them going.
It was learned-and I would not mention it here if it were not so-that a certain size of fish was not useful to the National Fish Company in their business. The gentleman in question obtained these fresh fish for little or nothing from the company, salted them down and sold them in the West Indies. But what did the poor fisherman get? He was not allowed even fair competition. He had to go out in his little boat alone, perhaps never to return, while the trawlers went out and brought in fish by the hundreds of thousands of pounds. It is the primary producer, the small fisherman, we desire to help, and each hon. member, if he does not sing his swan song in the meantime, will tell his electors what he did in the struggle on behalf of the primary producers of fish in the maritime provinces. I desire to say here and now that ever since I have been in public life, both in this parliament and in the legislature of Nova Scotia, I have always remembered one who was perhaps my greatest personal and political friend, one to whom I owe allegiance as a member of this government, the late Hon. George H. Murray. There was never an occasion when legislation which TMr. Finn.]
appeared to be in the interests of private individuals was introduced that I did not make it known openly and plainly just exactly what was my position. I tried to make it plain that the person I wanted to help was the man who had sent me there to look after his interests.

Mr. Speaker, I am interested in
this measure because of the long association I have had with several counties in Nova Scotia in which fishing is carried on. It seems to me that the principle of this bill is twofold. I agree that it is wise to appoint a board or other agency to study and report upon the best methods of preparing salt fish for the export markets, including the manner of curing and packing and the marking of packages for export, and arrangements for an adequate inspection of salt fish for export.
But these are matters which come within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud), and these studies might well be carried out under his supervision. With a board or without a board it would be quite possible I think to deal efficiently with these matters by means of an advisory committee, which could make its headquarters in Halifax, Lunenburg or elsewhere. There might be two or three committees for the several localities in Nova Scotia, because the fishing interests of one district are not entirely coincident with the fishing interests of another. That is a matter for careful study, and I would commend the Minister of Fisheries for taking any measures that he deemed advisable in order to effect the purpose he has in view.
But there is another minister who I think should be here to discuss this matter. The investigation of the marketing of salt fish in the export trade and the exploration of all the possibilities of opening up new marketing outlets is not a matter which immediately concerns the Minister of Fisheries. We have a Department of Trade and Commerce which has efficient and well qualified agents in the principal salt fish markets of the West Indies and South America, and they must have gathered clear and definite information with regard to the possibilities of improving our Canadian export markets in the ports under their jurisdiction. These are the men whose reports I should like to hear. The minister representing the Department of Trade and Commerce to which they are attached should also be heard as to the possibility of developing those markets for the salt fish trade. I remember very well, as a boy, when Yarmouth county, in which I was born, now represented by the hon. member for that county (Mr. Pottier) was engaged in every port and cove in building ships, large and small, and when there was an export trade in salt fish not only with the West Indies but with Brazil and even Argentina. But that trade has diminished until the market is almost lost. Whether the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier) gave a strictly accurate account of the loss of those markets I do not know. There are some conditions which occurred to me which were not stated by him.
But apart from studies and reports to the minister upon the best methods of preparing salt fish and packing and curing fish, and the adequate inspection of salt fish for export, this bill provides for a bonus to the exporter of salt fish; and it is quite clear that the hon. senior member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) was fairly correct in his summary of that provision. subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I move in amendment that we strike out the word- "salt." The idea is to make the act apply to all branches of the industry both salt and fresh. I listened yesterday and to-day to the many reasons put forward by hon. members from the maritimes as to why the bill should pass, and it surprises me that they always stop half way. If we desire to help the fishing industry of the maritimes, why should we take two bites at the cherry? Why not include the less in the greater? Let me suggest a parallel. Suppose there were an island on which the government desired very much to help in the establishment of an industry for the support of the inhabitants, and let us suppose they decided to start a saw mill. Suppose instructions were given, by virtue of the authority under which the mill was to be erected, that only fir should be cut by the mill, notwithstanding that there were spruce, hemlock and other kinds of timber. Somebody might come along and want to have some cedar cut. It might be said, "There is a good deal of cedar and hemlock on the ground and we could get rid of all that at the same time, and the overhead would not be more." But suppose the government replied, "No; youi authority extends to fir and fir alone." What success could anyone expect from an enterprise restricted in its operations to one phase of its possible capacity? Well, does not the fishing industry wish to do as much business as possible?

Salt Fish Board
I cannot see why there should be any objection to including fresh fish in this bill. If I were attempting to curtail the operations of this legislation I could understand an objection being raised, but that is not what I am doing; I want to extend the bill, and I cannot see that there is anything wrong in that. One would almost think that I had suggested something improper in asking that the bill be extended, that it be widened in its scope, with beneficial effects not only on the Pacific but on the Atlantic coast. I said yesterday, and it has not been denied- and it is obvious when we look back over the business of the past six years- that the trend is away from the salt fish industry and in the direction of fresh fish. The increased facilities of transportation, including airplanes and all the rest of it, favour the development of the fresh fish industry, and this is all the more accentuated by the comparatively recent disc'overy of a method of freezing fresh fish which makes it infinitely superior to the old system. Under the old system the freezing process broke down the particles and when the fish was thawed out it had to be used immediately and was not in the same condition as when caught. It was almost mushy. With the quick freezing process, however, the deterioriation is arrested at once-in fact it never sets in-and the fish is absolutely as good as when it was caught. The whole trend of the business indicates that we are progressing towards the handling of more and more fresh fish and the establishment of a fresh fish market.
It is as useless for us to try to build up a business when the trend of commerce is against it as it would have been for the old livery stable people to take the view that, whatever one might say about motor cars, they would continue to keep stables. In the long run the livery stable had to go, and the same thing will be true of the salt fish industry. Without depreciating their ability to handle salt fish-I am not doing that one iota-I do ask why this bill should not recognize the indisputable modern trend towards fresh fish. Why should not power be given to the board to deal with fresh fish? That is all I am asking-simply that they be given power to deal with the fresh fish angle as well, and as salt fish disappears or diminishes, we shall be able to control the business and switch over naturally and easily to fresh fish.
The bill declares that the object is to get more money for the industry. Well, suppose that in carrying out their duties the board discover that fish produced in a certain part of the maritimes could be better disposed of in the fresh fish market. Why should it be
wrong for them to have the power so to advise? But if this bill goes through as it is, it will be wrong, improper, ultra vires, for the board to make such a recommendation. Some particular bay or some part of the coast, from its proximity to a certain fresh fish market, might lend itself to the handling of fresh fish, but the board will be forbidden to deal with fresh fish at all under the bill as it stands.
I do not see that any harm would result from extending the scope of the bill so as to make it apply to both salt and fresh fish. They need not go into the fresh fish market if they do not think it necessary, but at any rate they should have the power to make recommendations in regard to fresh fish. It is said that this is one step in the right direction. Why not take two steps while you are at it? I repeat, it would not do any harm, and the machinery would be available, without the government having to come back to the house again, to enable them at any time to take such steps as they thought best with regard to fresh fish.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend that if we are erecting a board at all it is desirable to have one that has the power to deal with the fishing problem. Either it is intended to assist the fishermen engaged in the production and disposition of fish, or this bill is for the purpose of assisting those who are merchandising or exporting fish in the external trade.
It will be recalled that yesterday in the discussion one hon. member pointed out that there was a large production of fish and that a portion of the catch was salted and cured and exported in that form. If that is true, then the object of this legislation ought primarily to be to assist the fisherman who finds himself in possession of fish, of which only a part can be marketed fresh, the rest having to be disposed of in some other form. I suggest, therefore, that it is a mistake to start this movement with merely a salt fish board.
Let me refer the committee to the price spreads report, which went into this matter fully four or five years ago. There are one or two excerpts that may be illuminating and helpful. The report suggests the establishment of a board. This board, it says, might be known as the fisheries control board, and then it goes on:
Its most important duty would be to make every possible effort to ensure that the fisherman secure a fair price for his fish and not, as at present, the pittance that is left over from the consumers' dollar after all other branches of the industry have received their share.
That is the very essence of this problem- that the fisherman, the producer, may receive
Salt Fish Board

a better price for his fish. Nearly all the other factors that enter in, the processing, handling, marketing of fish, are conducted by business concerns. In the maritimes I understand that three large concerns do most of that business, and they are well able to look after themselves. Of course there are a large number in connection with salt fish. I take it that hon. members who are supporting this bill will assert that their object is to help the fisherman. If that is so, then the place to help the fisherman is back at the source or root of the matter, namely, where the fish are caught.
Then the report goes on to suggest certain other measures: the elimination of misrepresentation of varieties and grades, the establishment of higher standards of quality, adequate inspection of grades, the elimination of consignment shipments and of cut-throat competition, and the direction of surplus production of fish through channels calculated to bring the most profitable financial returns. There we have a tremendously important matter.
Those of us who have studied the question of marketing know that there is a large market in Canada to-day not properly and adequately supplied with fresh fish. There is room for expansion and extension of Canadian consumption of fish. The minister pointed out yesterday that one of the difficulties was the diminution in the demand for salt fish on the export market, that certain markets had been closed for one reason or another, that we had lost markets here and there. But the essence of the problem is in the handling of the fish from the moment it is caught. I suggest that the amendment of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni to strike out the word "salt," followed of course in subsequent clauses by consequential adjustments, would be advisable-that is, that the board shall be a fish board, to deal with the fish problem, with the marketing not only of salt fish but the marketing of fresh fish, because there is a lot of work that can be done there.
Let me add one observation; because I did not have an opportunity to speak on second reading-I was in the banking and commerce committee in another place. I am not criticizing the government for its effort to assist the maritime province fisheries and for leaving out British Columbia, because I believe that a certain proportion of the fishing population of the maritime provinces is perhaps in the most dire need of any class of people in Canada. I am not, therefore, begrudging any

assistance which can be given them, but that assistance I want to see reach the hands of the producer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I should like to offer the minister a suggestion. Yesterday when the bill was under discussion the meaning of the word "exporter" was questioned, and the house was assured that under the interpretation section "exporter" meant the person owning the fish. I shall read the definition as it appears in the bill and then offer the minister a suggestion which I think will clarify the meaning. The definition is:
In this act and in any regulation made thereunder, unless the context otherwise requires,-
(d) "exporter" means a person or cooperative group of fishermen owning fish which is afterwards exported in a salted state, whether dried, boneless, pickle cured or otherwise processed-
In the first place it is rather loose language, particularly the words "owning fish which is afterwards exported." The fisherman probably will part with his fish to a buyer, not knowing at all whether the fish are to be exported or sold in the domestic market. Then these fish are accumulated in warehouses; they lose their identity, and some go to the export market while others go to the local market, as conditions may dictate. Obviously it is impracticable for any board to follow that fish, unless the change we suggested a moment ago were adopted. That would make it allinclusive, and would deal with the original producer. But we are not doing that; we are dealing with the exporter, and the benefits of the bill cannot accrue until the fish are billed for export. Then the benefits accrue, but to whom? To the owner of the fish? Obviously you cannot follow the odd quintal of fish back to the original owner; it cannot and will not be done. In my opinion, and I am going to be very frank about this, the intention of the bill is to benefit the exporter, and no doubt it is hoped that the benefit to the exporter will be reflected back to the primary producer. Knowing business practices as I do, however, I venture to say that a very small modicum of this benefit or bonus will find its way back to the fishermen. I suggest that the definition be changed to read:
"Exporter" means a person or cooperative group of fishermen offering fish for export in a salted state-
And so on. In other words, after the fish are cured by the fisherman he offers them for export. Then the 'board takes the fish or directs the securing of them or controls them, and follows the fish through to the point of export. In that way you would segregate what was to be exported from what was to go on the local market, and you would have an opportunity of passing on a portion of the subsidy to the producer of that salt fish
Sail Fish Board

There is one other point. Where you have large exporting firms, at Halifax or other central points of shipment, it will be very easy to deal with the exporter of fish. But when you move along the coast of Nova Scotia towards the strait of Canso, in the area where the greatest suffering obtains among fishermen, the situation changes. There would be very small individual quantities of these fish made ready for shipment, unless you could get the fishermen working together in cooperative societies, which I agree would be a very desirable thing. In that case you might be able to follow the fish through, but as I understand it-and if I am wrong I am open to correction-the individual production is gathered up by coastwise boats and local concerns and moved to the export centre. I see nothing in this bill that enables this board to follow the fish back to the source of production. Therefore I am arguing very earnestly that what most of us have at heart, namely assistance to the producer of fish, will not be brought about by this bill. I offer this suggestion to the minister; I am not moving an amendment, but I suggest it as a possible improvement to this section.
