Yes. In some localities, as I say, the same person is the fisherman, the manufacturer or processor, and the exporter. In many other sections the fisherman does only a very small part of the processing and then turns over his fish to firms using the services of another class of people called the makers, whose job it is to dry the fish after it has 'been wet salted. There is also a third class of people interested in the salt fish business; that is, the final driers, and then the exporters put the finishing touches to the fish to prepare it for export.
My hon. friend said he had a suspicion that this measure had been framed for the purpose
[Mr. Stevens'
of giving help to the corporations, the big fellows, the well-known class of people called the exporters. I must tell him that the measure was framed with a desire to get away from that very thing. Had it been the desire of the framers of the act to help the corporations, we should not have gone to the trouble of trying to give an enlarged definition of the word "exporter." We would have simply allowed the word to carry its usually, accepted meaning. We went to considerable trouble to find a definition which would enable the board to give assistance to those who are spread along the coast, who catch their own fish, who put it through the first degree of processing, and who afterwards turn it over to others. We want the board to be in a position to give assistance to all three classes of people, if necessary. We do not want any one class to be overlooked.
To show that the meaning of the term is well understood by exporters I shall read to the committee a telegram I received the day after the bill was introduced in the house and reproduced in the Halifax newspapers. The bill was introduced on May 9, and on May 10 the following telegram was addressed from Halifax to the acting deputy minister of fisheries at Ottawa.
Board of trade telegram yesterday based newspaper report.
That sentence has no reference to this particular matter. Then the telegram continues:
Have just seen bill. Definition exporter ambiguous as under definition smallest fisherman becomes exporter if he owns even one pound fish which later is sold to dealer and exported. Actually salt fish exporters are corporation, individuals, etc., who conduct or intend to conduct more or less regular business of shipping salt fish abroad. Bill mentions board consulting committee on marketing. In addition committee clauses changed as formerly suggested word marketing should be deleted substituting consulting on any matter pertaining to work of board.
This telegram is signed by Fletcher S. Smith, president of the salt fish board of the Halifax board of trade. The telegram shows ' clearly that the professional exporters saw immediately the intention of the department in giving a special definition to the word "exporter'' as it appears in the bill. They protest against the definition which we have given. I undertook the responsibility of replying to that telegram in the following terms, on the same day:
Fletcher S. Smith, Esq.,
Halifax, Nova Scotia.
Your wire this date received. Do not agree that definition exporter is ambiguous, on the contrary made for purpose of covering small producer. Other suggestions to be taken into

Salt Fish Board
consideration. With regard wire yesterday, suggestions noted but am afraid cannot be entertained. The board is to be one for the benefit of the small producer as well as the dealer and exporter.
And this telegram is signed "J. E. Michaud, Minister of Fisheries." I am willing to admit that the definition of the word "exporter" is not as felicitous as it should be, and I am open for suggestions. I believe hon. members who represent constituencies made up of fishermen classified as salt fish fishermen will agree with me that if it is the intention of 'the measure to extend its benefits to these small people, then they cannot be defined as producers or primary producers. I defy anybody to tell me who would be a primary producer of salt fish. I should like to know when salt fish is produced or when it is finally produced. But I think by using the expression "owning fish which is afterwards exported in a salted state" the board is enabled to give assistance to small men who have been described as hook and line fishermen and inshore fishermen, men who live away out, long distances from communications, and have not the facilities for storing their fresh fish or for keeping them fresh until they can find markets. They must salt or process their fidh to some extent immediately after it is out of the water. We want to get at those men. If such a man puts a small quantity of salt on his fish, and that fish is afterwards exported, he is entitled to the benefits of this measure. The term "owner" has been used to enable the board to reach those men, and to have someone along the line who will handle 'the fish and extend a share of assistance to them. The term is also used to cover professional fish makers who are found along some, though not all, sections of the coast. They are not fishermen, but it is their business to take the wet and salted fish from the actual fishermen, and then to dry it, cure it and grossly pack it. Then they hand it over to another class of people who put the finishing touches on for export. Under the measure we want all three classes to be considered as exporters, because at one time they will own the fish and the board will be in a position to say that certain people are entitled to a percentage of assistance, whether it be twenty-five per cent or less. They may receive such share as may seem right and proper to the board in the circumstances.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
The processing of salt fish may have changed considerably since I was a lad in Nova Scotia. But I have been around the coast of Nova Scotia frequently in recent years during the summer holidays and have seen fish being pickled and in pickle, and
fish being salted and dried. I have reason to believe that the methods of processing have not changed very much in recent years in that branch of the fishing industry. What happens, I believe, is that the shore fisherman who brings in his fish may do one of two things. He may sell it at once to a company to be resold as fresh fish, in which case, either in ice or otherwise, the buyer prepares it for 'the market. There are certain processes which use salt and others which use chemicals to preserve it for the fresh fish market. But for the dried or salted fish market it is sold to a firm which packs fish as salted fish in barrels or hogsheads, or other containers in which the fish is finally sold after processing. That man or company is usually a person or firm distinct from the fisherman who actually caught the fish, hauled it into his boat and brought it to shore. In other cases, where fish is not salted when fresh and is not pickled, it is true that fishermen sometimes dry their fish. But a very small portion of the dried fish is dried by the fisherman or his family who caught the fish.
At different points along the coast I have seen considerable quantities of fish 'being prepared for the export as well as the domestic market. The person or firm having charge of the drying and preparing of this fish for export is not usually the fisherman who caught the fish. I am quite familiar with the counties of Queens, Shelburne and Lunenburg, and I know that in the olden days when most of the fish was caught from sailing vessels the fisherman was in a certain sense the owner.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: He is yet.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
When the fisherman fished from the vessel on shares, as he did in the olden days, he had an interest in the catch, which continued until the fish was dried. Often the owners of the fish or the managers of the vessel would have the fish dried and then sold for those who were working on that fishing vessel. But as I said this morning, this is not the way fishing has been conducted in more recent years along the coast of Halifax and Guysborough and as far east as the strait of Canso. Now a fisherman goes out in the morning in his boat, brings in his fish and sells it to a purchaser who intends to dispose of it on the fresh fish market; or he processes the fish slightly for the puipose of preserving it from the hot sun. The fisherman does not pack his fish in barrels or containers as salt fish, nor does he dry it for export.
I admit the difficulty which must have confronted the minister in the drafting of this bill, and I agree with the hoc. member for
Salt Fish Board

Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) when he says that when once the shore or boat fisherman lias caught the fish and brought it in, it is impossible to determine afterwards whether or not that particular fish enters the export trade. Under this bill it is impossible for the minister or the board to determine what portion of the fish caught by an individual or a group of individuals enters into the export trade. That difficulty must be met, and it is not met by this definition. If the definition in 2 (d) were that "exporter" means a fisherman or a cooperative group of fishermen owning fish which is afterwards exported in a salted state, then the individual fisherman or group of fishermen would be able to obtain a bounty under this legislation. But it is impossible by any practical business method to decide whether fish caught 'by a fisherman or a group of fishermen is or is not afterwards exported.
I know that a great deal of the fish that is caught and dried along the Digby coast is sold to various purchasers, the National Fish Company, for instance. I have seen fish spread out along that coast over wide areas for drying, and when I inquired who owned it,
I was told that such and such a company was the owner. The fish was being prepared for export in a special manner which would best suit the requirements of the trade. At that stage, when the fish is dried and ready for export, you can easily determine what portion is exported and what portion is sold on the domestic market, because the dealers could be compelled to keep accurate statistics as to whether it was sold in the domestic or in the foreign market. But when fish is caught by a particular fisherman in an open boat along the shore and brought in and sold partly as fresh fish and partly to those who intend to pickle it and partly to those who intend to dry and salt it for export, how you can determine the interest of that fisherman in the exported product is something I cannot conceive at the present time.
I think the minister will have to decide whether or not a bonus should be paid directly to the fisherman on his catch. This might assist very much in encouraging the fishing industry, because the bonus would be paid on the catch whether it were sold as fresh or as salted fish or whether it went into the export or domestic market. That would be the cleanest way of doing it. Once the fish enters into the ownership of a company which finally disposes of it by export, the company can very well show evidence as to the quantities of fish they have exported and with respect to which they will receive the bonus. That may assist the fishing industry.

As I said this morning, and as the hon. member for Kootenay East has emphasized this afternoon, while there might be moral grounds upon which a fisherman could demand some consideration from a firm of exporters because some of his fish was exported, or upon some other ground, there would be no legal ground upon which he could make such a demand. Once the money has gone out of the treasury with the approval of an order in council, with the approval of the board or of the minister, if it is paid to the man who is actually doing the exporting, who is the only man who can affirm that the fish has entered the export trade, I fear very little consideration will be given to the man who caught it, and who may be living miles or several hundreds of miles away from the port from which the export is made.
We are all anxious to assist these fishermen. As a matter of constitutional law, the fisheries are under the jurisdiction of this parliament, while the production of wheat and of many other things is not. If we can give and may give assistance to other producers who are not under the constitutional supervision and legislative control of this parliament, I see no reason why we should not give assistance to the fishermen whose business is under the control of this parliament. But I am loath to vote in favour of a bill that offers such scant advantage to the individual fisherman. I should like the minister to consider how you may determine that a fisherman once owned fish which is afterwards exported. We can easily tell who owns it at the time it is exported, but it is difficult to tell who owned it months before it was exported or even before it was fully prepared for export. I think the minister should reconsider that carefully.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I should like to say a few words in reply to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). There are two or three mistakes about the meaning of the bill in the minds of some hon. members. In the first place the bill is not necessarily a bonus-paying bill at all. The bill provides for assistance to fishermen.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: A quiet way of paying a bonus so as not to be offensive to competitors.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me, I will develop my argument. I am not speaking thoughtlessly or idly.
The assistance that is given to exporters of fish varies in different countries. In France I believe a rather large bonus is given to the exporter. In Norway substantial assistance is given to the producers or exporters of salt dried fish. In Newfoundland assistance is

Salt Fish Board
given, and while it is difficult to obtain the details of their plan it is something like this: There is a board, something like this board, I assume, which determines the minimum price which the producers of various grades of salt dried fish are to obtain; then theie are dealers licensed to buy this salt dried fish, and upon their export of the fish the loss to the dealers is made up out of the fund that is placed in the hands of the board. That is not a bonus in the ordinary sense of the term. It is the guarantee of a minimum price for the fish.
The reason for not being as definite as a great many members of the house would like the government to be is that exporters of salt dried fish from Canada are competing in foreign markets with exporters from other countries of this fish which is subsidized in various forms. The forms of subsidy vary from season to season and often from month to month, and if we were to draft and have parliament pass a bill which would say in detail just what assistance to our fishermen would be given by the government through the board, we would probably find that the form or extent of the assistance given by our competitors would be changed next month. That is the situation which necessitates an exceedingly flexible bill. It may be that one form of assistance will be given to one kind of salt fish, and another form of assistance to another kind of salt fish.
The point I want to make clear at the outset is that this is not a bill simply authorizing the payment of so much money per unit of the fish to any person-producer, exporter or dealer.
I cannot improve upon the explanation which my colleague the Minister of Fisheries gave of the scheme of the bill or the reason why "exporter" is defined as it is in the interpretation section. The word "exporter" is defined in such a way that any person and every person, whether fisherman or not, is eligible for assistance under this bill, provided only that the fish in respect of which assistance is given is eventually exported in a salted state from Canada. That is the definition, and believe me there was no hasty drafting of it. It was a definition drawn exactly for the purpose. If the definition, as suggested by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said, "a person, fisherman or cooperative group of fishermen" of course nobody could receive any assistance but the fisherman or the cooperative group of fishermen. But it may be important that the government be authorized to give assistance to somebody who gets the fish afterwards, on the condition or with the undertaking that he pass that on to the fishermen. It
would be impossible to do that for the very reason the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George advanced, the difficulties of identification.
The hon. member says that it would be impossible to trace the fish back. The government of Nova Scotia has been operating for the last two years a scheme which would come within the authority of this measure, and the assistance has been passed back to the fishermen. It has taken some little trouble to see that that was done, but it was done. Perhaps the payment of assistance will have to be somewhat delayed until it is ascertained to which country the fish is going; for I point out another thing: distinctions will have to be drawn in the treatment given fish exported to different countries. The United States, for instance, has a countervailing duty, and fish that goes into that country subsidized by the dominion government would get no benefit because it would be confronted by this countervailing duty. That does not apply to our fish going to Cuba, or Haiti, Brazil, or any of the other tropical countries which are and have been in the past such an important market for salted fish. This means that the board must exercise tremendous care from week to week, from day to day almost, to see that their form of assistance does not come into conflict with the laws of the countries to which the fish is exported. This is one of the reasons for having a board, instead of leaving it to the Department of Fisheries, whose head office is far removed from the place where this product is produced. The board will have to study the situation continuously and adapt their methods of assistance from day to day to the situation that arises, both in the countries of their competitors and in the countries to which the fish is exported.
Fresh fish, I might say, although it does not come under this bill, is exported from Canada almost wholly to the United States, and assistance to fresh fish would therefore be practically meaningless, almost useless. You could not give any assistance without doing yourself more harm than good, because the United States has a countervailing duty which could be applied to fish. But the same considerations do not apply to the export of salted fish. I read this interpellation clause to mean, and I do not think there is any doubt that it does mean, this:"'exporter' means a person .or cooperative group of fishermen owning fish which is afterwards exported" -by such person, group or anyone else; I read it as meaning nothing else-"in a salted state, whether dried, boneless, pickle cured or otherwise processed." If there is
Salt Fish Board

any doubt in the mind of any member that it has that meaning, I would take the responsibility of moving the insertion of those words, but I myself do not think there is the slightest doubt about it. What else could it mean? It means fish, whether salted or fresh, whether salted slightly or salted a lot, whether in the hands of the fisherman, the maker or the dealer, which is afterwards exported. That fish is eligible for assistance, all the persons who touch it are eligible for assistance, and the board has to see that the assistance is given in a way which will allow it to get back to the producer of the fish.
It is idle to say that the intention of the government is to assist some dealers or exporting corporations. Let us be practical. What government would do that or would want to do it? What advantage would there be to any government in doing it? Of course what the government is trying to do is to get the benefit back to the fishermen, but they will have to do it in a way that will be practicable in view of all the difficulties and the complexities of the situation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
What I have to say
is largely along the line of the remarks of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley). I do not think it is pretended that under this bill the individual fisherman will be subsidized for any one pound of fish which he may have caught and which will afterwards be exported. I do not think that would be feasible. In practice it could not be done. Undoubtedly what the government has in mind will raise the price not only of fish that is exported but of all fish, including even fresh fish sold in Canada, and that is as it should be; and if the bill can cover the three classes of people mentioned by the Minister of Fisheries I do not very well see that we can ask the government to go any further.
How will the individual fisherman be benefited indirectly? Let me refer the committee to section 5, paragraph (b). The board shall:
(b) devise and recommend to the minister a plan . . . with a view to . . . bringing greater returns to the primary producer and the exporter.
There is a misprint in that paragraph, by the way; "producer" appears as "produce." That refers to the producer whether he exports fish or not. What objection could there be to the board saying to the exporter, before paying any subsidy, "You must give the fisherman a quarter of a cent or a half a cent more"? That would not come directly under the act, but the whole fishing industry

would benefit, not only the exports but the fish sold in this country, even fresh fish. For any pound of fish exported would make room for a pound of fresh fish to be sold in this country.
With regard to the definition of "exporter," it seems to me there is an anomaly here:
"Exporter" means a person or cooperative group of fishermen owning fish which is afterwards exported. . . .
This covers the cooperative group but it seems to exclude the lone fisherman. What objection could there be to this phraseology: " 'exporter' means a fisherman or cooperative group of fishermen or any other person owning fish," and so forth.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: "A person" is a fisherman.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: It is true that "a person" is a fisherman, but in this context, since you have differentiated between person and cooperative group of fishermen, the definition would be interpreted as shutting out the lone fisherman. Why not say a fisherman or group of fishermen or any other person"?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: The Minister of National Revenue says that "a person" is a fisherman. Quite true. And this person you are dealing with here is a person owning fish which is afterwards exported. Our point is that you cannot determine that the fish caught by a given fisherman has 'been exported. It might be salt-cured and sold in the local market. This is the crux of the matter, because if you turn to subsequent sections you will find that the board is being empowered to give assistance to exporters, to make agreements with them. The interpretation clause is therefore important.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: It is vital.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Yes. Now let us examine this. Exporter means a person owning fish which is afterwards exported; exporter means also a cooperative group of fishermen owning fish which is afterwards exported. These two classes are clearly within the scope of the bill. In other words, all the large exporting firms are taken care of. They are covered. The cooperative societies are covered.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: And all persons.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
What we are getting at is this. We want to ensure that when this bill passes we are not going to be faced, through the interpretation of any section, with impediments to the giving of reasonable assistance to the very class referred to by the minister, namely, the primary producer, the fisherman who catches the fish. It is then green-cured,

Salt Fish Board
as some of us say, then dried, and so on. I am not an expert on fisheries but I do understand something about administering laws, and I apprehend that there will be all sorts of difficulty and that the board will have a great deal of trouble in paying the bonus, or the benefit, or whatever you choose to call it, to this class to which I have referred. That is the difficulty. All I ask is that in this interpretation clause we make it abundantly clear that these people will share in the benefits. There is $800,000 in the estimates to cover this. Knowing something about the export business and the general subject of merchandising, I know that the exporter as a concern, and the cooperative group as a concern, will take by long odds the lion's share. There is no question about their rights; they are clear. There will be no difficulty in paying them. Here is an exporter doing business in Spain. He says, "I am competing with Norway and Sweden and Newfoundland. The conditions are thus and so." The minister visualizes the setting up of a scheme to suit-whom? That exporter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Not at all; I did not say that, either.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I am not saying this in an offensive way.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Don't misrepresent me,
then.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
The minister is a trifle
too touchy. I am trying to clarify this complex matter. He said that in Norway and Sweden they gave certain types of benefits-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
And in Newfoundland
another type, and in other places others; and he said it was impossible to frame this bill in such a way as to meet all these contingencies. He said furthermore that one man might export to a market governed by certain conditions, another man might export to another market with other conditions, and there must be flexibility in the bill to meet these variations. Now that is all I say that the minister said.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That is all right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Let me come back to
where I was when the minister jumped off the roost for a moment. Here is an exporter exporting to Spain in competition with Norway and Sweden. That calls for the setting up of a certain type of assistance under the bill. That man is taken care of; the powers with respect to him are clear. Here is a man
exporting to Cuba and meeting the Newfoundland situation. All right; we will fix another form of assistance, and he is taken care of. But the man I am concerned about is the fisherman referred to by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. While I know a little about the technique of this thing; while I have been in the maritime provinces, have a reasonable amount of intelligence and can see for myself, I am thinking about these fishermen up the coast, who are remote from Lunenburg or Halifax, who have been abandoned by the big companies-there are packing plants up there that cost perhaps $100,000 or $150,000, shut down; the only place to which these people can send their fish to-day is the central markets, and that is why they are suffering. This is the class we want to assist. The minister rather taunted me a moment ago, saying that I did not understand the thing. I was not going into the details of how the fish is piled in the sunshine and dried and mild cured; it is not the business of parliament to analyse all that-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I did not mention the hon. member in the whole of my speech.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
Pardon me, the hon.
gentleman did; he said I did not know what I was talking about.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I did not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I am not pretending to deal with these details, but I know, and other hon. members know, that it is the class of fishermen remote from the large centres, not in direct contact with the large exporting firms, who are in difficulty to-day more than any others, and it is to ensure that that class receive the benefit that I am arguing this afternoon. I believe this section could be clarified. The word suggested by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Robichaud) would probably do it, covering the fisherman or smaller processor. Anyone who is familiar with the administration of these laws knows that the smaller man invariably disposes quickly of his catch or product-wheat, tomatoes, fish-whatever it may be. Why? Because he is living from hand to mouth and has to do it. He disposes of his product to the first person to whom he can sell in order to get a little cash to buy groceries, clothing and other necessities. The identity of the fish is lost. To say that you can set up a board with inspectors and officials who will follow that fish from the fisherman to the mild curer, to the salter and dry processor, and then to the man who trims it for final export, and keep its identity-it cannot be done.
Salt Fish Board

Futhermore a portion will be sold on the domestic market and a portion sold as salt fish.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Why not follow back the exported fish?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That is equally difficult. I will explain why. Let the experts correct me if I am wrong. This commodity is gathered into central depots for export, because it is exported in large numbers of barrels or boxes or kegs or in whatever form it may be packed. It may lie in the warehouse for some time; being .preserved or cured it does not have to be exported to-morrow. It may be several months before it is sent to market. Ii may be sent on consignment-I am not sure on this point, but I know that used to be done.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Not much of it now.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Then the returns have to come in, and you would not make up your claim for the benefit to be paid until that export is accomplished. In the meantime the fisherman, who is the one we want to help and whom we now have to search for like the needle in a haystack, sits twiddling his thumbs, waiting to see whether he shares in this or not. Again I say to the minister, out of some experience in this sort of thing, that it is the easiest thing in the world to lose sight of and forget these inarticulate and helpless people. I repeat, that is why I want to see in this bill a mandatory or obligatory instruction to the board that they shall look after that class, the small producer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I am glad to hear my hon. friend state at last that he is in perfect accord with the intent and purpose of this bill; because it is drawn and worded for the purpose of helping the very people he has been describing as remote and neglected and forgotten. The only point upon which we seem to disagree with regard to this definition of exporter is that according to my own interpretation I have always regarded a fisherman as a person. My hon. friend says he is not-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: No, the minister did not quite catch what I said. I did not say he was not a person. I said that under this definition the "person" is limited to a person owning fish which is afterwards exported. Therefore a fisherman, unless you can identify him with 'the export, does not become "a person" under this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Unless he owns fish he is not a person entitled to the benefit of this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Unless he owns fish which is afterwards exported; that is the qualification.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Exactly. All those who will be entitled to benefit under this bill will be persons who will at one time own fish which is exported. But there is no objection whatever, if it would serve the purpose of clarifying the meaning of this section, to using the word "fisherman," making it read: "'Exporter' means a person, a fisherman or cooperative group of fishermen."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Put the word "fisherman" first.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
It has been repeated
several times that- some fisherman might dispose of his fish, right after it is wet salted out of the water, to people who will finally process and export it. You cannot expect that fisherman to get all the benefit under the act and leave the others without any. In order to cover that class I am willing 'to include the word "fisherman," with groups of fishermen and other persons who may come under the act to be entitled to benefit.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That will help somewhat, but another problem follows. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Robichaud) approved by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), will improve the bill. But this problem arises and should be considered: the bonus or assistance granted from the public treasury should, according to the statement of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Usley), go primarily to the fisherman. The bill is intended to assist the fisherman.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Pardon me; the fisherman who will devote that part of his catch to export as salt fish.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Quite so; it is to the fisherman of the fish that is subsequently exported.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: In a salted state.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
The whole of the bonus- I persist in calling it a bonus; it is well known to what I refer-is to be distributed among those who actually fish and catch the fish subsequently exported. Now, the exporter acquires the fish, he keeps it in stock for months, as the hon. member for Kootenay East suggests, and then exports it. What is to be the rate of division between the fisherman or group of fishermen who catch the fish and the firm or corporation that actually exports the fish? If the entire amount is to be paid for the benefit of the fisherman or groups of fishermen, then nothing is left for

Salt Fish Board
the exporter, in case he is not a fisherman, but a company or a corporation engaged in the export business. After all, the export business is carried on by firms or companies, even though a firm may be a shareholder in the fishing schooner.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: They usually are.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: How are you to divide it? What is the proper share of the exporter?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That will be his lookout. We feel that the exporter can very well look after himself. Our purpose is to see that the exporter, if he is the one who actually receives the money, produces evidence to satisfy the board that he has paid either the fisherman or the fish maker, the secondary processor, a fair and reasonable portion of the final price. If he cannot do that, he will not be entitled to, and will not derive, any benefit.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I commend the minister for his good intentions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: It has been done in Nova Scotia for two years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That is a different situation. The government and legislature of Nova Scotia can control the prices of fish products in that province. This parliament cannot. Therefore the legislative power they have over all property and over all contracts relating to the sale and exchange of property places the provincial government and legislature in a supreme, a paramount position which is not occupied by this parliament, this government or the minister.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I agree with that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: For the moment I should be willing to accept the definition, improved as the hon. member for Kent has suggested, which suggestion has been approved by the hon. member for Kootenay East.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I have agreed to that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: But I shall renew the discussion when we reach section 6, because in voting an appropriation of $800,000 to be distributed under this act, parliament must prescribe definite conditions and regulations under which the bonus shall be apportioned or paid as between the respective contesting applicants for it. The exporter will allow very little to get out of his hands if he once receives the bonus, unless there are explicit terms regulating the action of the board in making payment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I confess that in reading this section, and especially the definition of the word "exporter," I was not clear as to what the minister had in mind. But since
he has explained that by "exporter" he means to include even a single fisherman, and I understand that the word "person" will include such fisherman, nevertheless, I think we should include the word "fisherman." Since we mention fishermen later, I believe we should mention the single fisherman. I have prepared an amendment which reads as follows:
That clause 2, paragraph (d), be amended by striking out the words "person or cooperative group of fishermen" and substituting therefor the words "fisherman or cooperative group of fishermen or any other person."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That is satisfactory.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I do not wish to raise undue
objection or to erect barriers to impede the passage of this measure, but in my opinion the whole purpose and intent of the bill, from the first clause to the last, is to help one class of person only, that is, the exporter.

speechtext:
Was the hon. gentleman
here w'hen the committee resumed at three o'clock?

speechtext:
There is no need of beating about the bush in connection with this matter. I am dealing more with the situation in Halifax, where to-day we have a concern known as General Sea Foods. It is a United States corporation, with its head office in New York and a branch office in Boston. They have moved everything that is movable out of the Halifax office, and little or nothing is known as to the reason. To be candid, in my judgment, and speaking subject to correction, one of the reasons for this bill is that during the past year, as the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of National Revenue know, when the question of fresh fish and the National Fish Company of Halifax was under discussion, they built four vessels. I am subject to correction by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, who is well versed in these matters, but he knows that for years the fleet which went down to the banks from Lunenburg had to lie idle in that harbour. They were beaten out in one matter, and now they are going to be beaten in a second matter by the National Fish Company, which practically controls the fresh fish business in Canada. Now they are going after the other market, and the person who will be frozen out, who will have to stand the gaff and take the hook, will be the poor fishermen along the coast of Nova Scotia and the county of Halifax. I shall not interfere with other constituencies, but will leave them to hon. members representing them.

who takes his life in his hands and sometimes never returns, and who has to leave his wife and helpless Children. The fisherman is like the man about whom the President of the United States has spoken; he is the man by the side of the monument, the forgotten man.

My learned and hon. friend, the Minister of National Revenue, is a keen lawyer, and able in his profession. I do not think he would turn out of his office a piece of legislation like this, or would offer it as a draft for the consideration of 245 members of the House of Commons. speechtext:
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Kent is a good amendment. It endeavours to protect as far as possible the class of person which we are desirous of protecting and assisting. We want to make his life and the lives of his wife and children happier as the days go by. We want to provide a little sunshine where there is fog, disaster and a great deal of sadness and sorrow. All you have to do is go into the constituency of my hon. colleague and myself and travel the 115 miles from Ecum Secum to Dartmouth, and the 40 miles from Halifax to Peggy's Cove, to realize the conditions under which these fishermen live. How can hon. members talk about these men being exporters? If you went down there and congratulated one of these men upon being an exporter, he would be so much surprised he would probably drop dead. As hon. members who represent fishing constituencies know, most of these men have not sufficient money with which to buy one of these little racks

Salt Fish Board
upon which codfish is dried. All that many of these men get is what they earn from shovelling snow through the winter. How is such a man to get into the export business? The only chance he would have is to make some sort of arrangement with the prime minister of England which would give him the right to trade umbrellas for fish.
I should like to see this matter stand over until to-morrow to see if it would not be possible to set up a subcommittee of hon. members of this house. Such a committee could discuss the matter with the minister and it would shorten up things and make them better all round. An endeavour should be made to see if more cogent clauses could not be drafted to cover the things which apparently it is desired that this bill should do; then put the bill through in a form which would mean something to the poor fisherman along our coast.
I commend this amendment. I want the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of National Revenue to understand that I am speaking in no spirit of criticism and with no desire to hurt anybody. I have but one aim and object, and that is to try to help the poor fisherman who to-day cannot help himself. If the parliament of Canada can do that without regulating him out of business, we shall at least be attempting to assist him and give him some hope for the future, a future that at its best is none too bright. That, sir, is my only motive. I have no interest in the matter except that I have always loved the poor man, the man who has to work by the sweat of his brow-and sometimes not only his brow is wet but his cheeks too, with tears. That is what is occurring to-day in Nova Scotia, and with all the resources which this government has at its disposal, when we can spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on commissions taking evidence in various matters, surely we can spend a little time in trying to do something for the poor fisherman. Perhaps we can get some expert or set of experts, practical men in the fishing business, to come before the minister or the officials of his department to give their views.
The minister said that no one had had anything to do with this bill except the officials of his department and himself. I do not think that is a sound position. I think any department, especially a technical department, could not have done better than to bring to Ottawa men honest in purpose and intention, men who are anxious to help the fishermen of Nova Scotia, to assist the minister in putting on the statute book practical 7H92-286
legislation that would mean something. Then the fishermen on next Christmas day would not find his sock with only a heel and toe in it. Under this measure, if passed as it is, he will get not only the toe but the boot.

The hon. member for Kent (Mr. Robichaud) told us a little while ago that he had had great doubts about the meaning of this subsection, but that after he had heard the explanation of the Minister of Fisheries he was convinced it was satisfactory. The hon. member for Kent is one of the ablest lawyers in the house, and when he has doubt about a thing there is room for doubt among those of us who are not lawyers. I am not a lawyer, and a lot of other people are not lawyers, and I do not want something in a statute which creates dubiety in the mind of a clever lawyer, but something that I and ordinary people can understand.
I got quite a kick this afternoon, to use the vernacular, from observing the change in popular sentiment, so to speak. Yesterday afternoon when I sprung on the house the idea that this was a bill primarily for the middleman a dozen members leapt to their feet, sword in hand, to convince me of my error. Outside of Grimm's Fairy Tales it would be difficult to find how many expenses they could pull out of a clear sky-expenses, con-

Then there was the collector, who collected the fish and centralized it in one place, the agent and the exporter. He said that all these people were entitled to a share in the bonus or the benefit. I distinctly take issue with that. I say that no middleman is entitled to any share in a bonus of that kind, because the middlemen have their charges paid, no matter whether the transaction is profitable or unprofitable to the producer. To come back to the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Robichaud). I have an amendment which I drew up an hour ago intending to propose it when an opportunity offered. I wish to extend somewhat the remarks I made before luncheon to-day.
I do not think this question of marketing and the survey of possible markets is a matter which should be under the supervision and jurisdiction of the Minister of Fisheries.

speechtext: It is not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has at the present time agents and officers in the chief markets for fish, and I have no doubt that an examination of his files will show quite recent reports as to the difficulties of marketing and the prospect of extending our markets, together with a statement of the countries competing in those markets and of the conditions which have enabled competing countries to drive Canadian fish out of those markets in foreign countries. I have before me the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1938, in which I find a complete and detailed report of the markets for fish. I find that markets for salt and dried fish are restricted largely to the West Indies and Cuba. At one time we had a market in Brazil, but that market has been restricted. The market in Cuba has been increased considerably. I find that in 1934 we shipped to Cuba 21,248 quintals; in 1935, 38,280 quintals; in 1936, 47,296 quintals; in 1937, 46,891 quintals, and in 1938, 39,800 quintals of dried and pickled fish. That really	is one	of the principal
markets for Canadian dried and salted fish. I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce, if he had an hour available to examine the statistics in his office, could give us a clear idea of the state of those markets and the adverse conditions which have restricted our sales there, although with the exception of the last year our sales to Cuba have been increasing; and he would be able to inform us also as to who are competing with us in those markets. We are asked to bonus our product in order that it may compete with the products of certain other countries. Which are those countries? How much of the market do others control? Do they control it because
Salt Fish Board

of -better shipping facilities? Do they control it by reason of having some advantage under the foreign tariff? Do they control it by reason of the rate of exchange that prevails? Before we enter upon a final discussion of this scheme we should have a review of the trade and commercial conditions with which we are dealing. Otherwise it is impossible for hon. members at least those who have no more intelligence than I, to appreciate the conditions and difficulties our fishermen are up against. That is a matter which always has been under the jurisdiction of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I doubt the expediency of taking it out from under the jurisdiction of that department.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: May I assure the hon. member for St. Lawrence^St. George and the committee at large that there is not the slightest intention of taking the promotion of the sale of fish, any more than that of the sale of any other commodity, from the Department of Trade and Commerce.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: This bill so states.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I must repeat my statement that there is no intention whatever of interfering with the functions of the Department of Trade and Commerce in connection with promoting the sale of any commodity whatever. It is, I think, pretty thoroughly understood by this time that it is strictly within the province of the Department of Trade and Commerce to promote the sale of all Canadian products in foreign countries.
I may tell the committee at once that I am not prepared to take an hour to make a statement in connection with the promotion of the sale of salt fish or any other kind of fish, or to discuss what is being done in connection with the promotion of sales in foreign countries. The bill was not in my charge; and while I have no desire whatever to evade my responsibility, I am not prepared to go into all sorts of details with regard to fidh. All hon. members know there are so many different ways of preparing fish and so . many fadtors entering into the preparation and sale of fish that the minister cannot be expected to know all the details offhand.
I might, however, give the committee a little information as to the markets to which Canada in the past has made sales of fish, and the difficulties in connection therewith.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: That was what I desired.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I shall give that to the best of my ability and as briefly as possible. As a matter of fact, the difficulties in the marketing of fish are similar to those we have experienced and are now experiencing in connection with * Mr. Cahan.]
the marketing of wheat. For instance, in some parts of Canada the fishermen are confined almost entirely to the production of this one commodity, and they are producing in excess of what can be consumed in this country. There is a necessity, therefore, just as there is in the case of wheat, of finding a foreign market. And just as in the case of wheat, we find we are confronted with certain difficulties, such as those of exchange control and tariffs, and particularly the difficulty of very severe competition from other countries.
The hon. member has asked who our competitors are, and has asked me to name our chief markets. In the past the chief markets for this kind of fish, or for fish generally, have been Italy; the West Indies, including Cuba; Spain and, particularly, Brazil. Our chief competitors are Newfoundland, Norway and Iceland. Newfoundland is perhaps as strong a competitor as we have. The people of Newfoundland are almost confined to the production of one commodity, namely fish, and it is true that they seem to be able to provide competition by selling their fish at a price lower than that at which we can sell. The result is that we are in keen competition with Newfoundland.
Then, some of those countries are trying to make barter deals. They are attempting to exchange their products for the products of other countries. Canada has never tried to enter into barter arrangements. It may become necessary so to do. Norway subsidizes heavily her exports of fish. I take it that this bill is by iway of providing some means of competition with Norwegian and other fish.
Italy and Brazil, to both of which we formerly sold large quantities of fish, are now trying to develop their own fish producing facilities. The same condition applies to fish as applies to wheat. Where in years gone by we sold large quantities of wheat to France, Germany and Italy, those countries are now in a, large measure supplying themselves. I am informed that Italy and Brazil are making determined efforts to supply their own fish. So far as Brazil is concerned, where we had perhaps the most valuable market of all, they have put on a very high tariff against Canadian fish.	.
I have spoken of some of the difficulties. The chief of these are the strong competition we have to meet, exchange and other controls, and other obstacles which have been placed in the way of trade. In that connection I might instance Italy. In recent years Italy has established a board which has complete control of all purchases, including purchases of fish. I believe at one time large quantities of Gaspe fish went to Italy. That fish

Salt Fish Board
was of the finest quality. But for reasons of their own the board which operates in Italy are buying fish which they can obtain cheaply from other countries-I think probably from Norway. Someone may say, "Why not try to make some sort of trade agreement with Italy?" May I point out to the committee that the former government was negotiating and had practically concluded arrangement of the terms of an agreement with Italy. We continued those negotiations; but as hon. members know very well, certain events made it practically impossible for us to negotiate with Italy. Those negotiations have not been concluded and are being resumed. At the same time, here is one difficulty. Unless by way of trade agreement Italy guarantees that she will make a definite purchase of our fish, there is not much that can be done, because there is no private purchaser of fish in Italy. All purchases are under the control of a board.
I believe I cannot add anything further. In speaking I have attempted to point out the competition we must face. I apologize to the committee for making my observations rather discursive.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
No, they are not; on the
contrary they are extremely interesting.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I have outlined the problem
with the information I was able to obtain a few moments before I spoke. I would say that we still have a good market in Cuba. Most of our market is in eastern Cuba, although in that market Newfoundland is now becoming a strong competitor. I believe the western end of Cuba is being supplied by Norway. One might say, "Well, if you can sell Canadian fish to eastern Cuba, why can you not sell it to western Cuba?" I am told Norway happens to have a particular method of curing fish which has special appeal to the people of western Cuba. As I said at the outset, there are, in connection with the preparation of fish many matters with which I am not familiar, but it will be realized that there are ways of preparing fish which will appeal to some groups which have been accustomed to a certain product. I believe the same is true in Brazil and in other countries.
Then, our market in the British West Indies is not as good as it was. Newfoundland has become a keen competitor. The committee is aware that we have had a twelve-year trade agreement with the British West Indies, and that it will be terminated at the end of this year. The government has given notice of the termination of the agreement, pending the making of a new agreement with the
British West Indies. We hope to have discussions, beginning perhaps late in the summer or early in the fall, with regard to the consummation of a new trade agreement. I can assure the committee that in those negotiations the Department of Trade and Commerce will bear in mind not only the conditions with respect to fish but those with respect to all other commodities, and in any negotiations will do everything it can to promote the sale of fish and other commodities.
At one time we had a market in Spain for fish. The reason for the loss of that market is at once evident. During the civil war in Spain very little could be done by way of carrying out an exchange of products. An additional reason is that some of those countries have become more or less impoverished, and have not the purchasing power they had before. In many instances they try to make barter arrangements, but, as I said before, Canada has not taken part in those arrangements.
If the hon. member would like to ask any further questions I should be pleased to give the best answer I can. Meantime I believe that is about all I can say.

speechtext:
I should like to have the opinion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, if he feels disposed to advance one, as to whether a bonus on the export of dried, pickled and salt fish is likely to increase our sales in the markets he has mentioned? For instance, I have these figures showing sales to Jamaica:

speechtext: Newfoundland was paying a higher commission to their agent in Jamaica.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
What country is competing with us and taking away our market in Jamaica? I know Jamaica very well, and I have no doubt the minister knows it equally well. I have been there on many occasions, and I must say I have never had salt fish prepared in as delicious a manner as I have had it in Jamaica or Trinidad. They seem to have facilities to make it a most delicious and tempting dish. What has interfered with our market in Jamaica? Is it Newfoundland? Does Newfoundland subsidize or assist exports *to Jamaica in such a way as to drive us from the market? Can we by a vote of $800,000 reestablish in those countries markets for the
Salt Fish Board

Canadian product? What are the prospects, because we do not wish to throw away $800,000? It is a large sum of money to be expended in one year. There are many primary industries which could be assisted by such a large appropriation as that. I should like to know if this $800,000, for the distribution and payment of which we are now providing by this bill, will reestablish our Canadian fish in the markets of Jamaica? There are other markets which might be considered. Despite competition, we have kept up pretty well in the Cuban market. Who are our competitors in Cuba? The minister suggests Norway.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: In eastern Cuba, and Newfoundland is becoming more and more a competitor in the west.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
To what extent are they subsidizing their dried salt fish and pickled fish in competition with us? Is a subsidy to our fish producers likely to reacquire these markets for us? I suppose Italy is beyond hope. In 1934 we sold Italy 76,505 quintals, in 1935, 70,597 quintals; in 1937 our sales had dropped to 1,404 quintals, and in 1938 they had dropped to nothing. Will subsidizing our producers serve to reestablish our market in Italy? Will subsidizing our exporters do it? Will it not be necessary to adopt other radical measures, such as the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggests? Will the matter not depend upon the improvement of relations between this country and Italy?
From my youth I have always looked upon Italy as being one of the foremost, friends of the British people. I was quite sorry to see this friendship disturbed, and possibly this disturbance has effected some reaction in the loss of our market for fish in that country. With what little knowledge I have, I cannot see how subsidizing the exporter of salt and pickled fish, as that exporter is now defined, is going to reestablish our market in Italy or increase our sales in Cuba, Jamaica and other parts of the West Indies. I have been in these countries quite frequently, and ever since I was a lad I have noted that our fish seemed to be much appreciated there. Whenever you were invited out to attend a government banquet or to the houses of some of the wealthier people, you always had placed before you a dish of salted or pickled fish. The people in these countries regarded that as the most tempting dish they could put before a visitor to whom they wished to show some special attention.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
My hon. friend asks me if it is my opinion that the granting of subsidies to our Canadian fishermen will increase our

sales. My answer is that to the extent to which you bonus the seller of fish, to that extent will he be able to compete in foreign markets. My hon. friend has also asked me who are our chief competitors. I mentioned before that Newfoundland is our greatest competitor in the British West Indies. I have no definite information with regard to Jamaica, but their sales in western Cuba, where we have always had a large market, are increasing. Newfoundland pays a bonus of $1 a quintal, which is a direct detriment to the exportation of Canadian fish. Last year Norway paid bonuses amounting to 7,000,000 kronen, but I do not know the exact value of the kronen.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Twenty-five cents.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
That is nearly $2,000,000. If the Canadian exporter must enter into competition with a bonus paid in another country, surely that is one reason to indicate that the payment of a bonus will give him greater opportunities in that market. I think the answer is obvious. If the Canadian fisherman is placed on a similar basis so far as government assistance is concerned, he should have some chance to compete in these foreign markets. It seems to me that is the answer. Personally I do not regard it as being desirable that we should bonus any commodity. I do not like the theory at all. I will be frank in saying that I do not like it in connection with wheat, but we have to do that because of difficulties which have arisen in western Canada. We have to do it in this instance in order to help the fishermen of Nova Scotia who are perhaps just as hard pressed as the wheat growers of western Canada.
I hope this will be a temporary condition. I hope conditions will improve so that these fishermen will be able to sell their fish on their own merits and make a living. In the meantime we have to deal with a condition, and this is an attempt to place the Canadian fishermen on a basis on which they will be able to compete with foreign producers of fish.
So far as Italy is concerned, I would say that perhaps there is considerable doubt as to whether a bonus will assist in that market unless we are able to negotiate a trade agreement. ' It will assist perhaps to the extent that the monopolistic board in Italy will be able to buy Canadian fish cheaper than they can be bought now. They may prefer to buy Canadian fish at the lower price, because of the bonus. If an agreement is made, one of the terms that should be insisted upon, in view of the monopolistic organization they have over there, is that they should buy a definite quantity of Canadian fish each year.

Salt Fish Board
I do not think I am disclosing any important secret when I say that is one of the obstacles to making a trade agreement with Italy.
I suppose it means that the Canadian government is helping the foreign consumer to obtain cheaper fish, but it is one way of relieving the present desperate situation, just as we are doing in western Canada. For my own part, I should like to see all these products able to stand on their own feet and compete on their own merits, but we have to deal with conditions as we find them, and this is one effort to deal with the fish industry in this country.

speechtext: I am grateful for the information the minister has given us because it tends to give us a broad view of the situation which was lacking before. I would point out that what has been emphasized in this debate as the ground for subsidizing or assisting or bonusing the Canadian fishery product is that it would give an increased price to the fishermen of this country: But I doubt whether the fishermen will receive very much of an increased price if the price level to our own producers is to be reduced in order that they may be able to compete with Norway and other countries which are subsidizing their products so greatly.

He will get more money if he sells more fish. But the situation in Nova Scotia, as I see it-this is not from immediate contact with the fishermen, although I was there last year and heard the matter discussed-is that in certain districts of that province where shore fishing from boats prevails, the fishermen seemed to feel that the more fish they caught the poorer they were because they have to spend time and money operating their boats and fishing gear, and they receive very low prices for the products of their fisheries.
There is one other question I would ask the minister. Is it not true that in one or more of the trade agreements which we have with other countries, to which we sell a certain quantity of dried and pickled fish, the bonusing of our fish or subsidizing or assisting it financially as this bill proposes to do-I am not particular what term you use-will lead to adverse reciprocal measures by those countries tending to protect their own markets against the subsidized or assisted Canadian product? I have not had an opportunity, while this bill was under discussion to-day, to look up the trade agreement with the 71492-287

Just to clear up the point raised by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George as to the effect of bonusing or assisting fish going to the United States, I have under my hand section 303 of the United States customs tariff, which reads:
Whenever any country, dependency, colony, province or other political subdivision of government, person, partnership, association, cartel, or corporation shall pay or bestow, directly or indirectly, any bounty or grant upon the manufacture or production or export of any article or merchandise manufactured or produced in such country, dependency, colony, province, or other political subdivision of government, and such article or merchandise is dutiable under the provisions of this act, then upon the importation of any such article or merchandise into the United States, whether the same shall be imported directly from the country of production or otherwise, and whether such article or merchandise is imported in the same condition as when exported from the country of production or has been changed in condition by re-manufacture or otherwise, there shall be levied and paid, in all such cases, in addition to the duties otherwise imposed by this act, an additional duty equal to the net amount of such bounty or grant, however the same be paid or bestowed. The Secretary of the Treasury shall from time to time ascertain and determine, or estimate, the net amount of each such bounty or grant, and shall declare the net amount so determined or estimated. The Secretary of the Treasury shall make all regulations he may deem necessary for the identification of such articles and merchandise and for the assessment and collection of such additional duties.
