Last night when the estimates were before the committee I undertook to furnish the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) with information on two matters: first, the number of postal meter machines in use in Canada, which is approximately 1,500; and second, information which I promised to place on Hansard giving details of air mail contracts entered into by the department in connection with air mail services in Canada. It is a lengthy document and to read it would be more confusing than enlightening. I would ask the consent of the committee to put it on Hansard.
Agreed.
One other question in regard to the air mail service. Can the minister give us any information regarding the transAtlantic service?

Perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver South would allow me to bring up first a matter which is akin to the question he has asked, and one answer would serve *both purposes. The minister, in his usual courteous manner, informed me last evening that he would revert to this question, notwithstanding that it comes under item 279, because I had intended to draw his attention to the air service as it affects the Atlantic. On January 19, I received through the mail a map published by the authority of John A. Sullivan, K.C., deputy postmaster general, showing the air mail service extending from Vancouver and carrying through to its eastern point in Montreal. I took occasion at that time to communicate with the Post Office Department because the map showed Canadian air mail routes in operation, indicated by a plain line, and Canadian routes proposed, indicated by a dotted line, 'but showing no part of Halifax. Halifax was not even mentioned either by name or in any other way. There was nothing to show that we were a part of Canada. I wrote to the deputy postmaster general as follows:
In to-day's mail I received a circular letter headed: Office of the district director of postal services, Ottawa, along with a map issued by the authority of yourself, showing Canada's air mail routes and I wish, as a representative from Nova Scotia, to lodge a very definite complaint of the construction of the map as once again Nova Scotia is entirely left out of the picture in so far as air mail routes are concerned.
This map will be issued to all parts of Canada and make known the fact that in so far as air mail is concerned, it will begin at the western coast with service at both Victoria and Vancouver, and stops in the east at Montreal, completely isolating New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia.
I feel that this certainly is an injustice to the Atlantic coast and the province bordering on the eastern portion of our dominion. Even though there may be no Canadian route in operation, I feel that the map should have shown with a dotted line, route proposed which would lead into Halifax, the eastern gateway of Canada, or some other mark denoting suggested line.
I am not in a position to know as to whether your scheme in connection with service has been completed, but I feel that if such is not the case, there certainly should be provision made for the complete coverage from east to west, extending from Halifax to Victoria.
Would appreciate you advising me in connection with this matter.
Along with the map there were a number of time-tables. I looked through the complete list-there were thirty-six of them- 
and not once did I see the name Halifax. I then consulted the index of places to be served, and running my finger down the H's I again failed to discover Halifax indicated as a part of Canada. Under date January 20 the Postmaster General replied in a letter, the second paragraph of which reads:
May I say in reply that the map to which you refer was issued principally for publicity purposes and was intended to make clear to the recipient the routes which were actually in operation at the time.
For publicity purposes! I suggest that in future the Post Office Department should be very careful in the issuing of maps. I received a further communication together with a map on the cover of which was "Effective March, 1939." I again took the question up with the present Postmaster General, and perhaps I should thank him for having discovered, since he assumed office, that in the eastern part of the dominion there is a place known as Halifax. He issued a new map effective April, 1939. Again I looked at the new map. He does show the name Halifax; he also prints a larger number of tables to show that the air service is advancing by leaps and bounds, and to-day instead of thirty-six it has gone up to something like sixty-four.
No, thirty-eight services.

Well, sixty-four routes. But again I fail to find Halifax, the gateway of eastern Canada, mentioned. I know the Postmaster General will keep in mind that he is serving the whole of Canada, that he will want to serve the east as well as the west. Along with the question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South, I ask that the Postmaster General be good enough to advise us when Halifax will be included in the actual air mail service.
Next sitting of the house!

It gives me the greatest pleasure to assure my hon. friend that Halifax will not be forgotten. The air mail necessarily follows the Trans-Canada air service, which of course requires landing fields. At present the landing fields are in course of construction. The eastern terminus of Trans-Canada Air Lines as is well known, is at present Moncton. It is contemplated that this service will go into effect on September 1- that must be taken only as an approximate date. But immediately it does, the air mail service will be extended to the various points in the maritimes, including Halifax and other points that can usefully be served. It would be inadvisable to mention a definite date, but I can assure the hon. member that air mail

Supply-Post Office
service will proceed to Halifax and other eastern points just as fast as circumstances permit. I understand that the Department of Transport is working energetically to complete the necessary landing fields to make that possible.
In reply to the question of the hon. member for Vancouver South as to the progress of the transatlantic air mail, yesterday in the British House of Commons it was announced by the under-secretary of state for dominion affairs that it was hoped that the Imperial Airways would start operation across the Atlantic some time during July. Pan-American Airways have already started-in fact they started last Saturday. It will be a matter of interest to the committee to know that air mail rate across the Atlantic has now been definitely agreed upon. Conversations have taken place between the postal administrations of Canada and the United States, which have worked together in an endeavour to fix the same rate from this side of the Atlantic. The rate agreed upon is 30 cents a half ounce from both countries. Pan-American Airways started a weekly service last Saturday. Imperial Airways will start in July, according to the announcement in the British House of Commons.

Under this item 280 which I once described as an omnibus item, embracing money order, postal note and savings bank business and many other items, I should like to make a few observations. The minister has probably not had an opportunity yet to consider the matter, but I should like to know if he is considering any long term new policy for the post office to expand its work to meet modern conditions, social, business, economic, patriotic, educational and so on, as the British post office is doing. The British post office is undertaking many new functions from time to time along the lines I have indicated. Take postal notes and savings banks; in my opinion there could be no little expansion of revenue to the department through the educational feature. For example, in the city I come from they have had, apart from the post office, a penny bank, to teach thrift and patriotism.
While our geographical conditions are different from those of Great Britain, I believe that in the future the post office could establish many features that would serve the public. It is a public utility, and every public utility has to be active in seeking to extend its services: light, power, telephone, transportation-the telephone is part of the British post office. You can bring to the people the services of the post office in many new spheres of activity, especially with the . geography
of Canada, three thousand miles from east to west or north to south. I believe that such a policy would lead to a large expansion of revenue, as in the case of the British and Australian post offices. Back in 1868 there were deficits. When Sir William Mulock became Postmaster General they had some surpluses, they started in 1902 with about 85,000; after the war they started to go a little in the red again.
Take, for example, education; many people have not a radio, many rural people have not telephones. I believe the post office, following the practice of the British post office, having a department which might be called a research department that would seek new spheres of activity not only in business but in social matters, health and other ways, in cooperation with the municipalities and provinces and especially the boards of education, would lead to a very large increase in revenue. The use of the post office is only in its infancy. Look at the cards used at Christmas and Easter, for birthdays and so on; many of them are manufactured in Germany and Japan. The new minister is wideawake; I believe he can bring a new vision and a new future for this great public utility and do much to develop the natural resources of the country. I hope that during the recess a study will be made to see if something can be done along the lines I have suggested.

Further than that, and while I am on my feet-I am sure the minister will realize that I am not referring to this or any particular government-we have been exceedingly lax in the publicity work done by our Post Office Department. Those of us who have been to the United Kingdom and who have had sufficient interest to investigate what is done by the British post office, know the splendid work of Sir Stephen Tallents, particularly in recent years. I would commend to the attention of the minister the work that is done there, and at the same time suggest that he give this item of $7,000 further consideration with a view to extending the publicity efforts of the Post Office Department.
Does the hon. member refer -to any particular service? The rates vary widely.
Any one of them.

It is anticipated that the rate of six cents an ounce which is charged in connection with the Trans-Canada air mail will, when that service arrives at the point where it is carrying 2,380 pounds a day, carry itself. Until -then the rate will not be sufficient to carry it. It is anticipated that the rate of six cents a half ounce which is charged on the all-empire service will carry itself. I believe it is anticipated that -the rate of 30 cents a half ounce which, as I stated previously, has been fixed for the transatlantic flight, will carry itself.

The reason I asked the question, and more or less following along the lines of the statement of the hon. member for Broadview, is that I have in mind the exceptionally fine publicity work that is done by the post office in the United Kingdom, publicity work designed not only to increase the use of the mails but to increase more intelligent use of the mails. I notice in the details of this item appearing on page 165 of the estimates that some $7,000 has been budgeted for publicity. I appreciate and agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood. I think heretofore the Post Office Department has under-advertised. After all is said and done, bearing in mind that this is the largest public utility in Canada, a certain amount must be spent in the way of advertising. Perhaps this department has spent less on advertising than any comparable public utility in this country. However, in reference to the item of $7,000 included under this vote, that is referable to the post office savings banks and not to the air mail at all.
I was referring to all mail.

Quite so. I was just explaining the reference to the $7,000 lest my hon. friend might think that was the total amount the Post Office Department was spending on advertising. Under the previous vote, 379, there is an item of $20,000 for advertising which is designed primarily to take care of the advertising incident to the inauguration of the air mail. I quite agree with the hon. member for Greenwood that, if anything, we have much under-advertised.

The splendid work that is being done by our tourist bureau is to a degree dependent upon the post office. After all, we have direct advertising by mail, which we have yet to develop to the fullest possible extent, and there seems to be a correlation between the two items. I commend to the minister's attention the possibility of using

more fully the excellent services of our tourist bureau and giving assistance there by way of expansion. [DOT]
Has the contract for the carriage of mails from Toronto to the Malton airport been entered into or executed as yet?

Yes; and I can tell the hon. member for Peel the circumstances as well. Tenders were called for the carriage of mail from the Malton airport to the post office in Toronto. Tenders were received. They varied in amount from, I think, $1,500, which was ridiculously low, to something like $6,000, which was the previous contract figure. I understand the distance involved in the yearly contract is something like 50,000 miles. When I went into the matter I found that Trans-Canada Air Lines, with which the postal service is definitely connected, had facilities which enabled it, without any additional capital cost and iby using surplus facilities, to carry the air mail from the Malton airport to the city of Toronto. In addition, there were four other places on the Trans-Canada air mail route where the same arrangement could be made, and consequently we made an arrangement with Trans-Canada Air Lines for, speaking from recollection, the sum of $10,500 to carry the air mail to and from these airports to the post office in each community. I had no hesitation in coming to the conclusion that this was in the public interest.

I should like to remind the minister that in this Dominion of Canada we have a city called Prince Rupert. I realize that the Postmaster General cannot attend to everything at once, but I should like to point out to him that air mail from Prince Rupert arrives here two days after the ordinary mail gets here. The minister gave the hon. member for New Westminster some figures in regard to the air mail at Vancouver, but these figures also include the air mail from Prince Rupert, which has to go down to Vancouver.
I believe the Minister of Transport has under consideration the feasibility of extending the service to central and northern British Columbia. Part of central British Columbia is now served by air mail, ibut the coast, where most of the population are located, is not served. We get mail from Fairbanks, Alaska, from the United States side two days quicker than we get it from the Canadian side. I believe this matter should be looked into, and I have no doubt that as soon as possible the Postmaster General will take some action. I am not complaining, because I realize that this is a new service. I believe we are as
air minded as the people of Vancouver or New Westminster. We feel that we are living in the dominion, and if the service is going to be extended to one community it should be extended to others, and especially to a port like Prince Rupert which offers the facilities of a railway terminus and a modern port. I would ask the minister to give the matter every consideration so that the facilities may be extended to that port.

The hon. member for Skeena, who has heretofore made many representations in connection with this matter, may rest assured that as soon as adequate facilities are provided in Prince Rupert, the Post Office Department will be only too glad to take advantage of them for the purpose of conveying air mail.

I should like to follow
up what has been said by some hon. members regarding opportunities offered to the Post Office Department to increase its services throughout the dominion. I have particular reference to the post office savings bank. I believe I have brought the savings bank to the attention of the committee at former sessions. Upon looking up the record of a few years back I find that from 1930 to 1937 there has been a gradual decline in the balance to the credit of depositors, and that it was not until last year that an increase was shown. In 1930 the balance stood at $26,086,036.03, and in 1938 it was $22,587,233.09. In the same manner the number of accounts declined until 1937, and then began to increase. In 1930 the number of accounts stood at 82,428, whereas in 1938 it was 84,118.
Until last year the number of post offices with savings bank departments had gradually declined. In 1930 there were 1,343, and in 1938 there were 1,362. The amount of interest paid by the Post Office Department on deposits decreased each year until last, when there was a slight increase. I am glad to note this turn of events. I believe one forward step which to a great extent has been responsible for the increase has been the change whereby a depositor was permitted to withdraw $100 a day. Formerly there was a limit of $50. If an improvement of that kind has brought about an all-round increase in one year, I should think it must certainly be encouraging for the Post Office Department further to increase its services to the public, and it will receive the proper support.
In the last ten or fifteen years there have been taking place in the dominion changes which, in my opinion, offer a great opportunity to the post office to give a service of
Supply-Post Office

which the public in many communities has been deprived. When I make that statement I am thinking of the banks which have pulled out of so many places and left the people without banking facilities. It seems to me that there is an opportunity for the Post Office Department to fill in that which is lacking. From 1920 to 1937 bank branches were closed in each of the provinces to the following extent:

Nova Scotia	 35
New Brunswick	 24
Quebec	 76
Ontario	  377
Manitoba	 180
Saskatchewan	 343
Alberta	 238
British Columbia	 54
In the Yukon there was an increase of one. These figures represent the closing of a total of 1,341 branches of banks between 1920 and 1937. I know that many of those branches may have been closed where there were two or three banks in one place. But there were many places where there was only one bank and, despite that fact, the bankers pulled out. As a result, people have had to drive thirty or forty miles to do their banking business.
I would ask the Postmaster General to consider the possibility of increasing the facilities of the post office savings bank to give accommodation to these people. I have in my hand a resolution passed by the delegates of district No. 12 of the Saskatchewan wheat pool in December last. It reads as follows:
Whereas the residents of rural and small urban communities are now almost entirely deprived of the services of certain functions of commercial banking through the withdrawal of branches of the chartered banks from these communities; and
Whereas the lack of these facilities make it necessary for our elevator department to appoint local payors with many attendant risks and inconveniences; and
Whereas the Post Office Department of Canada now performs certain financial services through their savings and annuity branches; and
Whereas the Bank of Canada Act authorizes the Bank of Canada to render to the people of Canada broad services through the monetary system; and
Whereas the purpose of the post office and the Bank of Canada is fundamentally to serve the people of Canada;
Therefore we, the delegates of district 12, hereby urge our board of directors to enter into negotiations with the proper governmental authorities to make it possible, through legislation or otherwise, for our rural and small urban post offices to render to their communities the services of commercial banking to the extent of deposits and withdrawals on current account, including chequing privileges.

That may be too big a step to [DOT]take at one time, but I suggest it is worthy of consideration.
There is a further suggestion I would make to the Postmaster General. In many instances branch banks have pulled out, leaving buildings with all the necessary facilities. I would suggest that the post office might utilize those buildings, because many of them are standing empty. They have all the necessary conveniences to carry on the work, and could be used to render a real service to the communities they would serve.
I am pleased to learn that an allowance for advertising has been set aside. I have noticed a general lack of knowledge regarding the post office savings bank. Many prominent citizens do not know of the services at their disposal. One may go into a post office and find only one card advertising the services of the savings bank department. At the present time there is no general attempt to pass on information to the general public informing them of the services at their disposal, and I am suggesting that those services should be better advertised. This would be one of the most convenient travelling aids people like ourselves could have. With a post office savings bank account, we could go into a post office anywhere in the dominion to withdraw what money we needed without having to pay exchange or anything else. It would not be necessary to carry round large sums of money.
There are one or two minor matters that I should like to suggest to the Postmaster General. The first is in connection with the passbook which has provision for only twenty entries. In my opinion the passbook should be larger. When the passbook is filled up, the postmaster has no authority to issue a new book. The old book must be sent to Ottawa when a new one is issued with the balance verified. I think the postmaster in a community should have authority to issue a new book, thus eliminating the wait of eight or ten days or two weeks that it takes to get one from Ottawa. Last year the former leader of the opposition appealed to the government to increase the interest rate paid on post office savings to 21 per cent. I think this increase in interest would encourage depositors to deposit their money, and the government would have a means of helping to carry on the finances of the country.
I should like to refer to one other matter which has been mentioned already in this discussion, namely, patronage. I have a letter here that I received from a man who had carried the mails under contract for eighteen years and three months. His contract expired

Supply-Trade-Commercial Intelligence
on December 31 last, but there was no renewal forwarded. The post office authorities told him to carry on because there must be some mistake, but his new contract did not come along. Then on March 31 he received word that his services would no longer be required and that a new man would be on duty the next morning. That is the only intimation he received after a service of eighteen years and three months. These things should not be.
I appreciate the constructive suggestions which have been made by the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Needham), and I can assure him they will receive every attention.

Item agreed to.
281. To compensate H. Marin, ex-mail contractor for financial loss resulting from falling off in amount of mail carried due to change in service, $2,088.32.

I have a few suggestions to make which I should like the Postmaster General to pass along to his colleagues in the cabinet. If certain changes were made and this department brought more in line with the British post office I am sure there would be increased revenue. First, the matter of tourist trade should be transferred to this department because this is really post office work. Matters having to do with radio should come under this department, as well as the advertising of natural resources and other matters of this kind. There would be reduced expenses if there was more coordination in this connection. It would eliminate considerable over-government, over-taxation and the appointment of useless commissions. The Post Office Department should carry out some of the provisions of the election laws, such as the sending out of postcards to electors as provided for in the new statute. In my opinion, if these matters were coordinated, considerable economy could be effected. They are really educational matters and belong in this department.

Some weeks ago we had under discussion the question of Japanese canned salmon being sold in Australia and Great Britain with the letters "CAN" on the top of the cans, the result being that the salmon was taken by the buyers to be Canadian salmon. At that time the minister was not able to give us much information, and I wonder if he has a statement to make to-night.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: As a matter of fact, at the time I said I had no information the department had already received notice of this and had taken up the matter with the British government. Mr. Hudd, chief Canadian trade commissioner in the United Kingdom, following some correspondence, brought the matter to the attention of the United Kingdom customs authorities. He now reports that this seeming violation of the United Kingdom Merchandise Marks Act has been noted and that warning will probably be issued to officers of the ports to watch out for possible similar future violations by Japanese salmon shippers If similar instances are found in the future the customs will probably insist that the qualifying mark of origin shall be equally conspicuous and indelible with the marks with which they are associated. Under the provisions of the merchandise marks act, however, it is not obligatory to state the country of origin and the use of the word "foreign" is sufficient for the purposes of the act. I think the matter is well in hand.
What about Australia?
Was not that in connection with labels?
No, the Japanese were doing the same thing in Australia; they were shipping in cans marked with the letters "CAN."
I did not think it applied to Australia. I thought the complaint was that the goods were being marked with wrong labels.
No, the minister will find that there were two complaints about Australia.

I see I have a memorandum on the matter here:
The Canadian trade commissioner at Sydney advised having protested to the Department of Health of New South Wales, who took the matter under careful review.
Samples of cans, and paper pressings of "CAN", in support of the above statement, were sent by the Department of Trade and Commerce to the Department of Fisheries at the time of their receipt. The Department of Fisheries replied that the whole Australian salmon situation had just been discussed (October 12, 1938) at a Vancouver meeting of the canned salmon section of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. As a result, it was decided to call a meeting of the entire canned salmon industry in order to take concrete action to correct reported irregularities in the Australian market. The Department of Trade and Commerce advised the Canadian trade commissioner in Sydney accordingly.
In January, 1939, the Canadian trade commissioner at Sydney cabled the Department of Trade and Commerce at Ottawa, that, while
4570	COMMONS
Supply-Trade-Commercial Intelligence
more similar shipments then in transit to Australia would be admitted, the embossed lettering "CAN" was now viewed as a contravention of the Commerce and Trade Description Act, and that future shipments must be marked indelibly "Produce of Union of Socialistic Soviet Republics in Asia." This cable was relayed to the Department of Fisheries and a copy sent to its chief supervisor at Vancouver.
We have every reason to believe that the action taken in Australia should put an end to the practice complained of.
There was also the matter of Canadian salmon being sold in Australia sometimes with a Japanese label, but that has been dealt with. It does not contravene the Australian regulations. As a matter of fact, much of our salmon is shipped without any indication of the country of origin, and importers in Australia put their own labels on. In some instances the labels were actually printed in Japan, but as they bore the words, "printed in Japan" they did not contravene the Australian regulations.

The other day I saw some
Japanese canned goods with the label printed entirely in English, and the name of a Vancouver firm on the label. That lettering, being all in heavy-type, gave one the impression that the fish was canned in British Columbia. But then in most inconspicuous type, so small as to be hardly noticeable, were the words, "packed in Japan." I do not know whether that is a way of overcoming the difficulty just referred to in regard to marking "CAN" on the tin, but evidently it is an evasion of the existing regulations. If there is going to be labeling of the place where the fish was packed so that the buyer can tell where it came from, it should be in type noticeable to the naked eye. I could easily procure some canned goods to show the minister how easily people can be fooled by labeling such as I mention, so inconspicuous as hardly to be noticed. If the regulation requiring the name of the country of origin to appear on the label can be overcome in this subtle way, I think the department should revise the regulations or at all events insist on the place where the goods were packed being printed conspicuously so that the buyer would know exactly where they came from.

That comes under the marking act, which is within the jurisdiction of the Department of National Revenue. I do not know whether the act prescribes the exact size of the lettering to be used, but I shall be glad to bring the matter to the attention of my colleague the Minister of National Revenue.

I think the hon. member for
Winnipeg North has reference to tuna fish because I doubt if any Japanese salmon comes * in here.
The reason for the importation of tuna fish is that we do not produce enough to supply our own requirements.

It is not a case of people
objecting to the labeling, but some people, if they knew the goods came from Japan, would not buy them, fish or any other commodity.

Personally I am inclined to
agree with my hon. friend. I am not declaring any policy, but I see no reason why any commodity that is imported should not, if it is at all possible, bear the name of the country of origin so that the Canadian people can decide whether they want to buy goods from that country or not. But that can be dealt with under the marking act, which is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Revenue.

378. Electricity and gas inspection services, including administration of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, $278,010.

In view of the cheap light and power movement in many of the provinces, would it not be well to reduce the cost of this inspection? In Ontario we have cheap light and power in the rural communities, but the cost of inspection of meters is a very large item of overhead. It seems to me that the government would be well advised to consider giving the inspection free. There is no profit from the system itself, because the power is supplied at cost, and this item of inspection imposes a very heavy burden on the consumer. I hope the minister can see his way to revising the schedule or reducing the inspection charge substantially.

It is always the intention that these services shall pay for themselves. This particular service pays for itself and has a substantial surplus. I shall be glad to take into consideration the possibility of making some slight cut. If I may revert to item 377 for a moment, Mr. Chairman, to say something kind about the department, I was

glad to hear some time ago about the splendid work performed by one of the department's officials in Sydney or Victoria, Australia.

S80. Motion picture bureau, $150,000.
What is the revenue of the bureau?
It is very small, only $18,000, but the expenditure is $74,000.
What is the reason for such a large increase this year?
That wretched bill we put through.

There will be some added expenditure owing to the activities we expect the film board to undertake. We are going to make some documentary films, which some hon. -members have urged and which we regard as highly proper. We expect to take over a good deal of the work which in the past has been done by various departments. There was some criticism in one newspaper, writing entirely in ignorance, to the effect that the various departments would continue with the same work they have always done, making their own films. That is exactly what we do not wish to have continued. The film -board has at its disposal an efficient plant for producing pictures, and it is the intention to take over the making of films from various departments. That means an added appropriation. I may say frankly that, with the formation of the film board, it is intended that its activities shall include the making of documentary and educational films. I am of opinion that there is great national work to be done in that direction. I am not intimating that we shall have an enormous increase in expenditures either this year or next year or so long as I am in charge of

Supply-Trade-Motion Pictures
the department, but I do believe that some added expenditure is entirely justified and will return good dividends nationally from the work that will be done. It is intended to make a documentary film, which is a part of the added cost, out of the material gathered in the course of the royal visit. It will make an interesting film comprising pictures taken throughout the country.
The minister is somewhat of an optimist when he says that other departments will lose their picture-making propensities.
Not entirely.

This afternoon he stood blandly in his place while we passed a bill which will substantially duplicate another branch of the department. A few weeks ago we passed bills under the auspices of the Department of Agriculture, one or two of them definitely encroaching upon and duplicating the work of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and here we are voting $150,000, an increase of $61,000, for the picture bureau. As I said when that bill was before us some time ago, the motion picture bureau then in existence was capable of carrying on the work, but we have superimposed upon that organization, at added public expense, two or three high-priced positions-at least they are to be provided for-
Only one.

-and I guarantee that next year or the year after,'when we come back, we shall find that very little additional work has been done. I am talking not about the number of reels, but about the official duties discharged. I venture to say that we shall find some departments carrying on subsidiary work which should be under this organization.
Some years ago parliament came to its senses and set up a bureau of statistics and a national research council. Let us take the latter particularly. The national research council took to itself all the scientific work that was being done in a haphazard way by half a dozen different departments. Mark you, Mr. Chairman, it was meant to abolish all duplication and to get rid of the rather inferior method of carrying on the work in the different departments. Parliament established the national research council and splendid laboratories were set up. But what is happening to-day? There is more clandestine scientific work being done by the departments outside the national research council than ever before. It is the old story. Any department or branch of a department

that can develop some little activity within itself, some duty or another which will help to make that branch grow, will do all it can to bring this about so that there will be more employees and the position of the chief will be aggrandized, thus bringing about an increase in salary. That is the whole psychology of the business. I am warning the minister now that by consenting to the invasion of the duties of the Department of Trade and Commerce by the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Fisheries, and by setting up this board with increased high salaried personnel, we are wasting public money and duplicating public service. This department over which he presides and the bureau which has been established for some time could have done all this work without that iniquitous bill which we passed a few weeks ago.

I do not propose to rehash the arguments I gave on the former occasion, as my hon. friend has done; he has repeated what he said when the bill was before the house. He makes predictions as to what is going to happen. I doubt very much whether he is right. When he speaks of the establishment of a number of high priced technicians he is very wide of the mark. The bill provides for only one additional paid employee. My hon. friend smiles skeptically at that; I can only say, as I think his leader said in connection with another matter, time will tell. The bill is put through in entire good faith, there is no ulterior motive; the whole purpose is to serve the country with a properly equipped film board which will take a wide view, make it its business to serve the country by the promotion of educational films and other activities. Other departments will have no power to act in respect of film making any longer except with the consent of that board. If that board does not do its duty, or if the officials connected with it do not do so, my hon. friend may prove right. My intention is that they shall do their duty, and it is my intention and that of the government to see that the men on that board are capable, qualified and earnest in doing the work they are supposed to do. If they are not, I shall be quite willing to abolish the board. In the meantime I believe it is going to do a very useful work.
Is that what the $61,000 extra is for?

Not all of it. Some of it is for salaries, provision of short-time employment on a fee paid basis of scenarists, directors, camera men, editors, technicians, et

Supply-Trade-Motion Pictures
cetera, for the production of special documentary, educational and trade publicity films; that amounts to $16,000.
Supplies, printing, stationery, et cetera photographic supplies, chemicals and so on- we must have equipment for use in the production of these films-$18,000.
Maintenance of present equipment, $1,000.
Express, freight, cartage, et cetera, transportation of equipment used in the production of these special series of films, $2,500.
Travelling expenses, $1,500.
Staff and experts in connection with educational and publicity films, $5,000, and some miscellaneous expenses.
When inaugurating the bureau, we have to have certain additional equipment and there are certain expenses to begin it. I make no apology for it; I believe we are going to get good value for the money, and if I happen to be here next year I hope to give an account of the expenditure of these moneys that will appeal to the members of the committee as having been in the best interests of the country.

I notice on page 192 of the estimates an item, "special personal services, $16,000." The minister stated a moment ago that there would be only one additional person hired on the extra appropriation. What is that $16,000 for?

In order to make these documentary films it may be necessary to hire experts; they may not have in the bureau now men who can do that work, and it will be necessary to hire experts for short periods. That is what the item is for.
Does the minister mean that in the list of persons referred to a moment ago, experts, et cetera, there is none capable of doing the work, that extra people have to be hired for it?

Quite so, and it may become necessary-I do not want to alarm the committee-to draw certain experts even from Hollywood; if there is a certain film which requires a certain technician that we must have, we propose to get him. The amount involved is not very large. For the work that can be done in the getting out of these educational and business promotion films this item is, I think, small, especially when one considers it in relation to some of the large amounts passed by this parliament.
Will it be necessary to bring in actors or actresses from Hollywood?
Is that a request for information, or the expression of a wish?

As the minister just said, in view of what can be done in this country I am of his opinion, that the increase in the estimate is very small in comparison with the value of that educational work. I had the pleasure of meeting the officer in charge of the motion pictures; they have interesting pictures which should be spread all over the country, if possible to every school in Canada to allow our children and youth to know their country. In my own case I had to wait until I became a member of parliament tc visit the west and the east. I am sure every hon. member will agree that there is no better means of education and acquiring knowledge than travelling and becoming acquainted with the people, the natural resources and the beauty of our country. I submit that this branch should be enlarged so that every school can have these films shown. For that purpose I suggest to the minister, if it is not already decided, that these films be made in 8, 16 and 32 millimetres.
We do that.

When the minister was
giving the details of this vote I was not able to follow him, it did not seem to agree with the details in the estimates. He said there was a small item for travelling expenses, I think $1,500-

but I should like the minister to explain how these films are distributed, whether they go out to the public, whether any charge is made for them, and who has the showing of them.

It really might come under the heading of advertising more than the making of films, because while it has some educational value, it also has a tremendous advertising value, particularly outside this country. With this increase we are asked to vote, how many extra films does the minister expect we shall have within a few years?

I am afraid I would not even like to commit myself to an approximation. 386. Administration, $106,754.

I have a suggestion to make to the minister. I do not know whether I am in order to make it at this time, but I shall be only a moment or two. What I have to say has to do with the commission now being charged for selling grain. I understand the grain exchange set their own tariffs. I would ask the minister to keep my suggestion in mind, and that the new supervisor for the grain exchange might be asked to consult with the grain exchange to see whether a change cannot be made.
At the present time the commission for selling wheat is one cent a bushel, and it is the same for barley, while for oats it is five-eighths of a cent a bushel. I believe the average carload of grain weighs 90,000 pounds. This would mean that it would contain 1,500 bushels of wheat, and would leave the commission for selling that carload of wheat at the sum of $15. The same car containing barley would contain 1,875 bushels, and at the present rate of commission the selling charge would be $18.75. A car of wheat at the present price of 80 cents a bushel Fort William, would be worth $1,200 to the farmer, and a car of barley would be worth only about $750. The car of barley is worth to the farmer approximately two-thirds of the value of the car of wheat, and yet he is charged $3.75 more commission for selling it. It seems to me that the same bookkeeping entries would be necessary on the sale of each car. My suggestion would be that the commission be reduced from one cent a bushel to three-quarters of a cent a bushel on barley. In that way it would be almost on a par with wheat. Precedent is found in the fact that at one time one cent a bushel was charged for the selling of oats, but now only five-eighths of a cent is charged. It is true that the amount is not very great, but it does amount to about $5 a car-and that is a worth-while saving, when one has to buy new boots for the baby. Canada produces, on an average, about 80.000,000 bushels of barley a year. So it will be seen that in the aggregate quite a sum would be saved to the farmers who grow barley. I would ask the minister to take this matter up with the grain exchange and see whether the commission could not be reduced from one cent a bushel to three-quarters of a cent a bushel for the selling of barley.
I shall be glad to consider what the hon. member has suggested.

I should like to associate myself with the suggestion of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. Perhaps I would be disposed to go even a little farther. I

have handled a great deal of grain in the last twenty years, through operating an elevator, and I do not believe that the grain men at Winnipeg are giving sufficient service for this commission. They could easily reduce the commission on wheat to three-quarters of a cent, on barley to five-eighths of a cent and on oats to half a cent a bushel.
. There is one other matter I should like to suggest to the minister. At the present time this payment is not called a commission but is described as a service charge, and it is paid to the grain firms and elevator companies for handling the grain. I think they are not entitled to those payments. The board gets the grain. Once it is delivered to the elevator it becomes the property of the board. All a grain firm can do to earn the service charge is to hand over the papers in Winnipeg, after the grain is shipped from the interior, and take them to the offices of the board. The grain then belongs to the board, which sells it. I do not think the elevator men or the grain commission firms-some of them are registered as commission firms, are entitled to that service charge. I do not know why they have changed the name from "commission" to "service charge," but the latter is what it is now called. I think the minister would be well advised to have different arrangements made between the grain firms and the board whereby the board would not pay a full cent-whether it be called a service charge or a commission-because no real service is given, compared with what was done formerly. When a grain firm used to take grain from a farmer, that firm was responsible for inspection and weighing, seeing that everything was in proper order, and transferring the money to the farmer after all expenses were paid. But as I understand the situation at the present time, the original document is handed to the board, and they are the ones who are entitled to any charge which could be made against the grain for selling. I heartily concur in the suggestion of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie.
I shall be glad to give consideration to what the hon. member has said.

I suppose a substantial part of this appropriation will be for the exhibit at the world's fair in New York. I am wondering what the value of these exhibits at international fairs really is. I have attended some of them in different places and that question has often occurred to me. In the exhibit that Canada is showing in New York we shall have to compete with all the larger countries which are spending ever so much more money than we are, far more than we could afford to spend, and far more than we ought to spend in this way. Apart from the ordinary competition which our exhibit will find in the larger nations, there is also the great attraction of the side-shows, which, it seems, are more important to the vast majority of the people who visit exhibitions than are the exhibits of the various countries. On the opening day of the world's fair in New York there was almost a riot because the side-shows were not open, and one can hardly dare suppose that because the Canadian exhibit had not opened on the first day there would be any riot.
Hardly any of the others were opened either.

That emphasizes my point.
I have visited these exhibitions in the past and gone to the buildings representing various nations, and I have come away wondering whether the vast majority of the people who attend these fairs really go for the purpose of getting some information regarding the countries exhibiting or for an altogether different reason. It is true that a goodly number of visitors may inspect the exhibits of Canada and other countries, but in view of the enormous amount of money we are spending and the comparatively small showing we are making in relation to other countries that are exhibiting, would the minister be good
enough to give us a frank opinion on this question? We are spending a large sum of money, and it is a question whether we should be more conspicuous by our absence than by the exhibit we have there.

I am sure my hon. friend
will hardly expect me, when we are authorizing an expenditure of some $400,000 for an exhibit at that fair, to say that the money is not well spent. I can understand the mental attitude of my hon. friend because I have sometimes been in the same frame of mind myself. But the doubt he suggests in regard to the value of this exhibit applies to all advertising. No one can detect and identify any particular benefit accruing from newspaper advertising, for instance, especially if it is general. We advertise the natural resources of the country; we advertise our railways; the Departments of Mines and Resources, Agriculture, Fisheries and others all advertise to the world at large what we are producing, and it would be difficult to estimate-certainly it could not be done in dollars and cents- the resultant value to Canada. In my opinion this advertising has a considerable value. Take the tourist bureau advertising the beauties and attractions of Canada. Many people are ignorant of those attractions, and this advertising will bring a definite return in the form of tourist business. I must not forget to mention that the provinces are also exhibiting their own resources.
I am afraid, not speaking strictly from the practical or utilitarian point of view, it would be embarrassing to us if our good neighbour to the south did not find us sharing at least to some extent in their great world exhibition. It is true also that compared with some of the larger countries Canada cannot make quite the showing that they are making; and I must say that while kind words have been spoken of our exhibit, there has also been some criticism that it is not as impressive as that of Great Britain or even of Russia or of Italy, and some other countries who are spending anywhere from three to five million dollars. Those things are all very necessary, of course, but Canada means a great deal more than that, and when I go to another country I like to see something more than that advertised. At the time of the coronation I remember very well that that magnificent store on Oxford street, Selfridge's, had wonderful plaques on all corners illustrating the various parts of the empire. I was particularly struck with the Canadian plaque, which was some thirty to forty feet high and perhaps almost as wide. After looking it over, I began to wonder if I really came from Canada. I saw on the plaque a number of pine trees with a goat among them; some totem polgs; an Indian dressed in his native clothes, complete with shawl and everything else; a hunter with a cap pulled down over his ears so that his face could not be seen, which would indicate that this must be a very cold country; a gentleman on logs in a river; dogs that looked like Eskimo dogs, and finally a Canadian mountie. Canada means a great deal more than that. That sort of thing is all very well, but I take the stand that when we exhibit or advertise in other countries we should tell the people that this is a thoroughly settled country. I believe western Ontario is about as thickly settled as most parts of the old country, with the exception of the townships and counties adjacent to the large cities. But according to all this advertising we are just producers of raw and farm products. We manufacture finished articles here also, and when the department advertises again I should like it to devote some part of that advertising to the products of the million or more workers in industry in this country. I know it is not the sole purpose of the Department of Trade and Commerce to stimulate the export of farm products; but if that should become the purpose of the department, then we had better create an industrial department for the purpose of seeing to it that industrial products are also exported.
When I was in the old country I made the best survey I could among manufacturers and others, visiting various boards of one kind and another, and I was very much surprised to read in a magazine called The Rubber Age, of May, 1937, the report of one of the big rubber manufacturing companies of Great Britain. In this report I found an opinion expressed that I discovered to be fairly prevalent in the old country, that Canadian manufacturing is just branch manufacturing, and that when you buy in Canada you merely

buy from the branch of a United States company, which means that in so doing you are not being patriotic towards the old country manufacturer. That is not a correct opinion, and I am convinced that the department should make a strong effort to convince the people of Great Britain that we are not just a branch manufacturing country, though even the branch companies are very large concerns in this country, employing thousands of workmen. I think it worth while to put this report on record, for the information of the department:
This group, which embraces footwear, general rubber goods, garments and sports goods, plays an important and increasing part in the broadening of the company's basis to which I have referred. The improved results from this group in recent years are a most encouraging feature of our operations.
Unfortunately, we still continue to suffer from severe competition from British territories overseas. You will remember that the chairman has more than once referred to the competition in rubber footwear from British territories in the far east, where very low standards of living and wage levels prevail.
We also suffer from the dumping in this country of Canadian made goods, some of which are sold here at prices below prices in the Canadian market.
I am told that is not so, but this annual report might lead one to believe that Canada is a low-wage country. As a matter of fact the wages in our rubber factories are well on to twice as high as the wages paid in the rubber industry of the old land. Furthermore, I discovered on investigation that many of the employees of the rubber industry in the old country start at fourteen years of age, and that seventeen and eighteen are considered fairly substantial ages. In this country one cannot start to work at less than sixteen years of age, so the age level here is not nearly as low as it is in the rubber industry of the old country.
That was the impression I obtained over there. It seemed to me there was an organized campaign to spread the idea that Canadian industry was largely an American branch manufacturing industry, whereas actually it is not. Listening to him, I would judge that his chief complaint is that the department is advertising only farm products or food products, and that it has made no effort to advertise manufactured products in Great Britain. I felt that while it was quite all right to advertise products of the farm, there was no reason, if it were possible to do so efficiently, why some government money might not well be spent to promote the sale of manufactured commodities. In this year's estimates there is an item of $100,000 for that purpose.
I would add, also-and perhaps the hon. member will be surprised when I say this-[DOT] that a year or so ago I wrote to the manufacturers of certain commodities in this country which are exported in large quantities, and in my communication I suggested that the department would like to cooperate with them in advertising their goods. I would add that it is perhaps somewhat more difficult to advertise manufactured products than food products. For instance, lumber might be classified as a manufactured product. It is pretty difficult to advertise Canadian lumber effectively. It may be advertised in a magazine or newspaper in any way you like, but when a man goes to a lumber yard I would imagine he does not 
know whether he is buying Canadian lumber or lumber from Norway or Russia. That is one difficulty.
The hon. member will understand that it is quite impossible for the federal government to advertise the product of any one factory; we simply cannot do that. Our advertising must be of a class. We cannot do that. It is somewhat more difficult to do that kind of advertising in connection with manufactured products than in connection with food products. I hope what I have said to the committee and to my hon. friend will convince him that the department accepts as one of its duties that of promoting the sale of manufactured products, in addition to the promotion of the sale of food products.

The question I was going to ask is this: This vote is headed " Mail subsidies and steamship subventions." How much of this vote is subsidies and how much is subventions? In the case of a mail subsidy, I assume we get a service and the subsidy is part payment. To what extent is it a subvention?

There is no segregation made as to what is subsidy and what is being provided for carrying the mails. All these contracts provide that the mails shall be carried without any further cost. For example, the Canadian Pacific has a total subsidy this year of $350,000 for carrying the mails on the

Atlantic, and the value of carrying the mails is $182,000. So the straight subsidy is not very large.
On the Atlantic are there several companies carrying the mail, and, if so, how is the money apportioned?
It is all Canadian Pacific.
No other lines carry the mail?
We have no other Ca.nadian line subsidized.
Are the Canadian Pacific steamships a Canadian line?

It is called the Canadian Pacific.
Mr. KINLEY': I am told that they cannot take on Canadians, that the British seamen's union will not allow them to be taken on British ships.
The ships are registered in Great Britain; that is true.

This vote is quite a
large one. Has the government this year made any inquiry, before arranging for the subsidy, as to wages and working conditions on these ships? I think it is the policy of this as well as of past governments that when a public work or a public service is assisted out of the national treasury, certain conditions as to work and wages are stipulated. Is the same principle followed in connection with these subsidies and subventions?

There is in the contract for
local services a clause which provides:
All officers and men and other persons employed on the vessel or vessels engaged in the performance of the subsidized service set forth in this contract shall be paid such wages as are generally accepted as current from time to time during the continuance of this contract for competent employees in the district in which the said service is being performed, for the character or class of work in which they are respectively engaged.
That is for local services?

Yes; it is not included in
the ocean services.

A few years ago the industrial and international relations committee went fully into this question as it affects the Pacific services and made certain definite recommendations. Those recommendations were unanimous, if my memory serves me aright-I was a member of the committee-and I would ask if the government has any intention of giving effect to
any of those recommendations or of taking steps to see that reasonable wages and working conditions are put into effect on these ships. It is understood that the Canadian Pacific employs oriental labour on its vessels because it is cheaper than white labour. But I do not think this government should subsidize oriental labour. If the company was employing labour that was in a position to demand reasonable wages and reasonable working conditions approximating, say, those maintained on United States ships in the same class of service, there might be some reason for paying a subvention or subsidy, but under present conditions I do not see why in the world we pay them.

It is almost eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and I wanted to discuss the general question of subsidies and how the various amounts are arrived at by the department. These estimates show that $2,054,000 is to be voted in subsidies and subventions for the coming year. In item 396, for instance, there is a subsidy of $600,000 for the service between Canada, China and Japan; $300,000 for the service between Canada and New Zealand; other items of $15,000 and $10,000, for other services; and $118,000 for the service between British Columbia and China and Australia. What is the basis for arriving at these amounts? Perhaps the minister would tell us either this evening or on some other occasion when these estimates are before the committee.

Subsidies are granted on the
general theory of promoting the sale of our goods in other countries. Many of these ships would not operate if they were not assisted, because they could not make sufficient profit. The whole question of subsidies may be a matter of opinion. So far as I am concerned, I do not like the idea of subsidies at all. I would like to see every tub stand on its qwn bottom-I did not intend a pun or to refer to any of these ships as being tubs. As I say, I do not like the idea of subsidies at all, but in order to sell our goods in other countries-and it is necessary that we do-there must be means of transportation supplied, and these services could not carry on, it is contended, without our supplementing the rates in this way.
As to how the amount is arrived at, in most instances tenders are called for. Not always, but where we find the service is properly rendered and there is no other line of steamships available we often give the contract again at

Naturally, especially if subventions and subsidies are going round.

It is a matter of opinion,
but in the interests of foreign trade we think it is advisable to supplement the revenues of these ships in this way.
